conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the unifying physiology linking steroid equivalents and sick day rules?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Exogenous steroids → negative feedback → HPA suppression → the adrenal glands stop making cortisol → the patient can't respond to physiological stress → risk of adrenal (Addisonian) crisis.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: On which three axes do the key glucocorticoids differ from one another?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Glucocorticoid (anti-inflammatory) potency, mineralocorticoid (salt/water) effect, and duration of action.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: State the equivalent doses of hydrocortisone, prednisolone, dexamethasone, and methylprednisolone.
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Hydrocortisone 20 mg = prednisolone 5 mg = methylprednisolone 4 mg = dexamethasone 750 micrograms. Doses below 1 mg are always written in micrograms, never as a decimal of a milligram.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Describe the mineralocorticoid effect, duration, and typical use of hydrocortisone.
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: High (salt-retaining) mineralocorticoid effect; short duration; used for adrenal replacement (mimics cortisol) and IV in crisis.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Describe the mineralocorticoid effect, duration, and typical use of prednisolone.
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Moderate mineralocorticoid effect; intermediate duration; the workhorse oral anti-inflammatory (e.g. asthma, PMR/GCA, IBD).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Describe the mineralocorticoid effect, duration, and typical use of dexamethasone.
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Minimal mineralocorticoid effect; long duration; used where fluid retention is unwanted — e.g. cerebral oedema, antiemetic, croup.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Describe the mineralocorticoid effect, duration, and typical use of methylprednisolone.
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Low mineralocorticoid effect; intermediate duration; used for IV pulse therapy.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: In terms of relative potency, how do prednisolone and dexamethasone compare to hydrocortisone?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Prednisolone is roughly 4× hydrocortisone potency; dexamethasone is the most potent (~25–30×) and the longest-acting.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Why is hydrocortisone the steroid of choice in adrenal insufficiency and crisis?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: It has significant salt-retaining (mineralocorticoid) activity, which is the effect you want in adrenal insufficiency, and it is given IV in crisis.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Why is dexamethasone chosen where fluid retention would be harmful, and what dosing convenience does it offer?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: It has negligible mineralocorticoid effect, so it's chosen where fluid retention would harm (e.g. raised ICP / cerebral oedema); its long duration suits single daily dosing.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the approximate physiological replacement dose of hydrocortisone?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Approximately 15–25 mg/day, given in divided doses.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the mechanism of HPA axis suppression by exogenous glucocorticoids?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH → adrenal atrophy → endogenous cortisol production stops.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Who is at risk of HPA suppression by the NHS Steroid Emergency Card threshold?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Anyone on prednisolone ≥5 mg/day (or equivalent) for ≥4 weeks — across all routes (oral, inhaled, topical, intranasal); also high-dose inhaled (beclometasone >1000 micrograms/day or fluticasone >500 micrograms/day).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the consequence of HPA suppression when a patient faces physiological stress?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: A suppressed patient cannot increase cortisol in response to stress (illness, surgery, trauma) without extra steroid → adrenal crisis.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the purpose of the NHS Steroid Emergency Card?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: It is issued to at-risk patients so that any treating clinician knows they need stress-dose cover. Patients with adrenal insufficiency are also supplied with an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit — the 100 mg IM dose may be given by the patient, a relative or a carer, and there is no risk of overdose in an emergency.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the underlying principle behind sick day rules?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Physiological stress normally triples-or-more cortisol output; the suppressed patient must take this extra steroid exogenously.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Sick day rules: what is the action for (a) minor illness with no fever and (b) illness with fever / moderate illness?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: (a) Minor illness / no fever — usual dose, no change, but double if bed-bound, needing antibiotics, or after significant trauma. (b) Illness with fever / moderate illness — double the usual oral dose for the duration of the illness and until 24–48h after recovery; seek review if it lasts more than 3 days.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Sick day rules: does a patient already on prednisolone ≥15 mg/day need additional sick-day dosing?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: No extra dose is needed for a febrile illness — they are already above the stress dose. Those on 5–15 mg/day should take prednisolone 10 mg twice daily. Vomiting, surgery or shock still require parenteral hydrocortisone at any oral dose.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Sick day rules: what is the action if a patient is vomiting / can't keep tablets down, or has persistent vomiting / diarrhoea?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Vomiting / can't keep tablets down → hydrocortisone 100 mg IM (or IV) from the emergency injection kit + seek urgent help. Persistent vomiting / diarrhoea → 999 / Emergency Department because of the risk of crisis.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Sick day rules: what steroid cover is needed for surgery or a major procedure?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: IV hydrocortisone cover, arranged with the anaesthetic team.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: During significant stress, what minimum steroid dose should be given until the illness resolves?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: At least 40 mg oral hydrocortisone/day in divided doses (or ≥10 mg oral prednisolone/day) until the illness resolves.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What three things should every steroid-dependent patient be told to do?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Carry the Steroid Emergency Card, double the dose when febrile (unless already on prednisolone 15 mg/day or more), and switch to the 100 mg IM hydrocortisone injection if vomiting.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How does an adrenal crisis present?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Hypotension/shock, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and reduced consciousness — in a steroid-dependent patient who is ill, stressed, or has missed doses. Hyperkalaemia is a feature of primary adrenal insufficiency, where aldosterone is also lost; in steroid-induced (secondary) insufficiency aldosterone is preserved, so the potassium is usually normal.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the immediate management of an adrenal crisis?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Don't wait to confirm: hydrocortisone 100 mg IM/IV immediately (adult dose), then 200 mg/24h infusion (or 50 mg 6-hourly) + IV 0.9% sodium chloride + treat hypoglycaemia. A cortisol sample may be taken at the same cannulation but must never delay the hydrocortisone. Call for senior help and admit.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Why must long-term steroids never be stopped abruptly?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: The suppressed axis can't immediately resume cortisol production, so abrupt cessation precipitates adrenal insufficiency.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: When is gradual tapering of steroids particularly important, and what other risk does abrupt stopping carry?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Taper gradually to let the HPA axis recover — reduce quickly down to about prednisolone 7.5 mg/day, then slowly — especially after >3 weeks of treatment, high doses (more than 40 mg prednisolone daily for over a week), or repeated courses. Another reason not to stop abruptly is rebound of the underlying disease.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What withdrawal considerations apply below physiological-equivalent steroid doses?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Below physiological-equivalent doses, hydrocortisone's shorter half-life may aid recovery; expect temporary withdrawal symptoms such as fatigue, low appetite, and low mood.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Why are prescribing errors usually approached as a system problem rather than an individual failing?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Errors are usually a systems failure, not individual incompetence — so the response is to fix the system rather than blame the person for honest error. Recklessness and deliberate violations still carry individual accountability.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: List the steps to work through before writing any prescription.
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: 1) Clarify the indication (is a drug actually needed?); 2) Take a full drug history (current + recent meds, incl. OTC + herbal — medication reconciliation); 3) Check allergies + prior ADRs; 4) Consider patient factors (age, pregnancy, renal/hepatic/cardiac function, genetics, comorbidity); 5) Check interactions (look them up in BNF); 6) Choose effective, safe, cost-effective drugs (right drug, dose, route, frequency, duration); 7) Share the decision (patient ideas/concerns/expectations, informed consent); 8) Write the prescription clearly; 9) Monitor + review (efficacy, ADRs, when to stop; deprescribe where appropriate).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Why should generic (non-proprietary) drug names be used when prescribing?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: They reduce confusion and reconciliation errors.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Dangerous-abbreviation rule: how should 'micrograms' and 'nanograms' be written, and why?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Write them in full — never 'mcg' or 'µg', which can be misread as mg.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Dangerous-abbreviation rule: how should 'units' be written, and what is the risk if abbreviated?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Write 'units' in full — never 'U', which can be misread as a zero, causing a 10× insulin overdose.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How should doses and units be written on a prescription?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: No trailing zeros (write '2 mg' not '2.0 mg'). Doses of 1 g or more in grams; under 1 g in milligrams (500 mg, not 0.5 g); under 1 mg in micrograms (500 micrograms, not 0.5 mg). Use a decimal point only where unavoidable, and then with a leading zero ('0.5 mL' not '.5 mL'). Write 'micrograms' and 'nanograms' in full, and 'units' in full for insulin and heparin.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What baseline requirements make a written prescription legible and legally sound?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Patient identifiers (name, date of birth, NHS/hospital number; address, and age if under 12, on an FP10), and the weight where dosing is weight-based; legible and indelible, or electronic; signed and dated; generic name, written in block capitals by convention for legibility; route, frequency, duration/quantity; max dose and minimum interval for PRN; allergy status documented, recording the nature of the reaction rather than just ticking a box.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What additional legal requirements apply when prescribing controlled drugs?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: The prescription must state the form; the strength where more than one exists; the dose (clearly specified, but it need not be in words and figures); and the total quantity or number of dosage units in both words and figures. It is valid for 28 days from the date on the prescription.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Classify prescribing errors by stage of the medication process, with an example error at each stage.
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Prescribing → wrong drug/dose/route/frequency, missed interaction/allergy, illegible. Dispensing → wrong drug selected, labelling error. Administration → wrong patient/dose/time/route, omitted dose. Monitoring → failure to monitor levels/function (e.g. INR, gentamicin, U&Es).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: In Reason's taxonomy, what is a 'mistake' and how does it differ from a 'slip'?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: A mistake is the wrong plan (knowledge/rule-based) — e.g. prescribing the wrong drug for the condition. A slip is the right plan but wrong action (attention lapse) — e.g. writing the wrong dose by accident.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: In Reason's taxonomy, define a 'lapse' and a 'violation'.
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Lapse = memory failure, e.g. forgetting to prescribe a needed drug. Violation = deliberate deviation from a known rule.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What does the mnemonic 'A PINCH' stand for (high-risk medications causing disproportionate harm)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: An Australian mnemonic (there is no equivalent UK acronym): Anti-infectives, Potassium and other electrolytes, Insulin, Narcotics (opioids) and other sedatives, Chemotherapy, Heparin and other anticoagulants.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Why is insulin a high-risk medication in terms of prescribing error?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Its 'U' abbreviation can be misread, leading to a 10× dose.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Give the specific high-risk prescribing pitfalls for methotrexate and potassium.
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Methotrexate — weekly, not daily (a classic fatal error): prescribe one strength only (2.5 mg tablets), specify the day of the week, folic acid on a different day, with FBC, LFTs and U&Es monitored. Potassium — never give as an IV bolus: give it diluted by infusion, not normally faster than 10 mmol/hour or above 40 mmol/L peripherally, using pre-mixed bags, never made up on the ward (cross-ref electrolytes).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which high-risk drugs require therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM), and why are anticoagulants and opioids hazardous?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Gentamicin and vancomycin need TDM. Anticoagulants (warfarin/heparin) → risk of bleeding. Opioids → risk of respiratory depression.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Explain the Swiss cheese model (Reason) of why errors happen.
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Errors result from multiple latent system failures lining up — defences have 'holes' that occasionally align — rather than a single person's mistake.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the key contributing factors to prescribing errors?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Inadequate knowledge/training, an incomplete drug history, poor communication/handover, fatigue + workload (on-call prescribing), look-alike/sound-alike drugs, trade names, and distraction.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is a 'just culture' approach to errors?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Honest error is treated as a system problem — focus on what went wrong, not who — so that staff report and learn rather than conceal. It is not a blanket 'no-blame' culture: recklessness and deliberate violations still carry individual accountability.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which intervention most reliably prevents medicines being omitted or duplicated at admission and discharge, and what are its three steps?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Medication reconciliation, especially at admission/discharge transitions. Three steps: verify (accurate drug history) → clarify (appropriate drugs/doses) → reconcile (document changes). (NICE) recommends it within 24 hours of admission to an acute setting, or sooner if clinically necessary. It is most reliable when pharmacist-led.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What tools support medication review and deprescribing, particularly in the elderly?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: STOPP/START — the tool generally used in the UK — and, from US practice, the Beers criteria, used to identify inappropriate prescribing in the elderly (esp. polypharmacy).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What system-level safeguards help prevent prescribing errors (besides reconciliation and review)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Electronic prescribing (ePMA) with decision support (interaction/allergy/dose alerts) — though it introduces its own errors, such as picking the adjacent drug or strength from a drop-down, alert fatigue and uncritical acceptance of default doses; double-checking high-risk drugs; standardised processes; BNF/protocols; and reporting + learning — local incident reporting (e.g. Datix) feeding the national Learn from Patient Safety Events service, the Yellow Card scheme for suspected ADRs, and Never Events. Incident reporting and Yellow Card are different systems, and one event may need both.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are 'Never Events' in the context of prescribing, with examples?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Wholly preventable patient safety incidents, for which strong national barriers already exist — e.g. wrong-route chemotherapy, insulin overdose from an abbreviation, or methotrexate overdose in non-cancer treatment.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the two main routes of drug elimination, and what happens if either is impaired?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Kidney = excretion (water-soluble drugs + metabolites), liver = metabolism. Impair either and drugs/active metabolites accumulate → toxicity.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What two things about a drug determine whether it needs dose adjustment in organ impairment?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: How is it cleared — renal vs hepatic? How narrow is its therapeutic window? Together these determine whether dose adjustment matters.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How does each ADME step affect drug handling in organ impairment?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Absorption: gut oedema, altered first-pass → variable bioavailability. Distribution: ↓albumin (liver/nephrotic) → more free (active) drug for protein-bound drugs. Metabolism: liver impairment → ↓clearance of hepatically-metabolised drugs. Excretion: kidney impairment → ↓clearance of renally-excreted drugs.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the core mechanism of toxicity in organ impairment?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Impairment → ↓clearance → ↑plasma level + prolonged half-life → accumulation → toxicity, unless dose/interval is adjusted.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Who is at risk of needing renal dose adjustment, and how do you adjust?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: At risk: drugs that are renally excreted (especially unchanged), have active renally-cleared metabolites, and/or a narrow therapeutic index. How to adjust: reduce the dose and/or lengthen the dosing interval; some drugs are contraindicated below a certain eGFR.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is renal function assessed for dosing, and when is eGFR unreliable?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: eGFR is the usual measure, but DOACs, aminoglycosides and digoxin must be dosed on creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault), not eGFR — eGFR is normalised to a body surface area of 1.73 m² and CrCl is not, so in small, elderly or very obese patients eGFR overstates true clearance and leads to overdosing. eGFR is also unreliable in AKI (not at steady state) and at extremes of body habitus.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How are aminoglycosides (gentamicin) and vancomycin handled in renal impairment?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Aminoglycosides (gentamicin): nephrotoxic + ototoxic; renally cleared → monitor levels. For once-daily regimens the level is taken 6–14 h after the first dose; for multiple-daily regimens after 3–4 doses — check earlier and more often in renal impairment. Vancomycin: nephrotoxic, narrow window → TDM.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is metformin handled in renal impairment?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Accumulates → lactic acidosis. Review the dose at eGFR 30–44 (max 1 g/day; do not start below 45); stop at eGFR under 30 and in AKI; withhold during any acute dehydrating illness.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How are lithium and digoxin handled in renal impairment?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Both have a narrow window → toxicity → TDM.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How are DOACs / LMWH handled in renal impairment?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Accumulate → bleeding risk. All DOAC thresholds are CrCl, not eGFR: apixaban avoided if CrCl under 15, and in AF reduced to 2.5 mg BD if CrCl 15–29 or if two of (age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or more); rivaroxaban 15 mg OD if CrCl 15–49, avoided under 15; edoxaban 30 mg OD if CrCl 15–50, avoided under 15; dabigatran contraindicated if CrCl under 30. LMWH accumulates from CrCl under 30 — reduce the treatment dose (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg once daily), monitor anti-Xa, or use unfractionated heparin.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Why is morphine avoided in renal impairment, and what is used instead?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Active renally-excreted metabolite accumulates → toxicity. Use oxycodone at a reduced dose in mild-moderate impairment; in severe impairment (eGFR under 30) oxycodone also accumulates — use alfentanil, fentanyl or buprenorphine.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How are methotrexate, allopurinol, and many antibiotics handled in renal impairment?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Renally cleared → reduce/avoid.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which drugs should be withheld in AKI, and which of them are actually nephrotoxic?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: 'AADN': ACEi/ARB, Aminoglycosides, Diuretics, NSAIDs (the commonly used UK sick-day version is DAMN — Diuretics, ACEi/ARB, Metformin, NSAIDs, plus SGLT2 inhibitors). Only aminoglycosides and NSAIDs are directly nephrotoxic; ACEi/ARB and diuretics impair renal perfusion, so they are withheld during the acute illness and restarted on recovery, not stopped for good. The 'may need to stop' list (metformin, lithium, digoxin) also applies — these accumulate rather than damage the kidney.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Why is hepatic dose adjustment harder than renal?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: There's no 'eGFR for the liver' — use clinical severity (Child-Pugh), LFTs, and synthetic function (albumin, INR, bilirubin) as a guide, rather than a clean number to dose against.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How do reduced first-pass metabolism and reduced drug-metabolising enzymes affect dosing in liver disease?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: ↓First-pass metabolism → ↑bioavailability of orally-administered, highly-extracted drugs → effectively higher dose. ↓Drug-metabolising enzymes → reduced clearance of hepatically-metabolised drugs → accumulation.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How do reduced albumin and reduced clotting factor synthesis affect drugs in liver disease?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: ↓Albumin synthesis → more free (active) drug for highly protein-bound drugs. ↓Clotting factor synthesis → exaggerated anticoagulant effect (warfarin).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the effect of portosystemic shunting on drug handling?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Drugs bypass hepatic metabolism; risk of precipitating hepatic encephalopathy.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the concerns with paracetamol, statins, and warfarin in liver disease?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Paracetamol: dose-dependent hepatotoxicity, but still the analgesic of choice in cirrhosis, since NSAIDs and opioids are far more dangerous — reduce the maximum to 2–3 g/24 h in decompensated cirrhosis or body weight under 50 kg. Statins: rarely hepatotoxic → LFT monitoring at baseline, 3 and 12 months; do not withhold or stop for mildly raised transaminases (under 3× the upper limit of normal), but avoid in active liver disease and decompensated cirrhosis. Warfarin: exaggerated effect (↓clotting factor synthesis).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Why are sedatives/opioids/benzodiazepines used cautiously in liver disease?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: They can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy — use cautiously.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which drugs are hepatotoxic and should be used cautiously in liver disease?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Methotrexate, valproate, amiodarone; anti-TB drugs (isoniazid/rifampicin/pyrazinamide).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which drug categories should be avoided/used cautiously in liver disease (esp. cirrhosis), and why?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Sedating drugs (encephalopathy), constipating drugs (constipation precipitates encephalopathy), NSAIDs (fluid retention → worsen ascites + hepatorenal syndrome, GI bleed), and hepatotoxins.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the general safe-prescribing principles in organ impairment?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Start low, go slow (lowest effective dose, titrate cautiously); avoid nephrotoxic/hepatotoxic drugs where an alternative exists; monitor organ function + TDM for narrow-index drugs; do not stop ACEi/ARB reflexively, as they are renoprotective in stable proteinuric CKD and a fall in eGFR of up to 25% or a rise in creatinine of up to 30% after starting is acceptable (NICE); check the BNF's renal and hepatic impairment guidance and the individual drug monographs; review the whole drug chart in any patient with new organ impairment (medicines reconciliation).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which four narrow-therapeutic-index drugs require therapeutic drug monitoring in renal impairment?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Gentamicin, vancomycin, lithium, digoxin.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is bioavailability (F), and what factors affect absorption?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Bioavailability (F) = AUC(oral) / AUC(IV) for the same dose (otherwise correct for the dose difference); IV = 100% by definition. Factors affecting absorption: drug solubility/charge, gut pH, blood flow, transit time.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is first-pass metabolism, and which drugs have high first-pass? What bypasses it?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Oral drugs metabolised in the gut wall + liver before reaching the systemic circulation. High first-pass = low oral bioavailability (morphine, propranolol, TCAs, GTN and isosorbide dinitrate — but not isosorbide mononitrate, which has ~100% oral bioavailability, which is why it is the oral nitrate). Buccal/sublingual routes bypass first-pass metabolism (GTN, buprenorphine).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is volume of distribution (Vd), and how do low vs high Vd differ?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Vd = amount of drug in the body / plasma concentration. It is an apparent, theoretical volume, not a real body compartment. Low Vd → stays in plasma (heparin, warfarin — highly protein-bound). High Vd → distributes widely into tissues (amiodarone, chloroquine, digoxin), with values far exceeding total body water. Factors: protein binding (albumin), lipid solubility, tissue affinity, BBB, placenta.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are Phase 1 and Phase 2 metabolism?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Phase 1: catabolic (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) — CYP450 enzymes; converts drug to a more polar metabolite. Phase 2: anabolic (conjugation — glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation); produces a water-soluble conjugate for renal excretion. Some drugs are prodrugs converted to active form (codeine → morphine, azathioprine → 6-MP).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is first-order kinetics?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Rate of elimination proportional to concentration; a constant fraction eliminated per unit time; 4–5 half-lives to reach steady state; 5 half-lives = <5% drug remaining.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is zero-order kinetics, and which drugs follow it?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Constant amount eliminated per unit time (independent of concentration); the metabolic pathway is saturated, so the concentration rises disproportionately — a small dose increase produces a large, unpredictable jump in level. Examples — PASTA: Phenytoin, Aspirin/Salicylates (high dose — A and S are the same agent), Theophylline, Alcohol. Phenytoin saturates within the therapeutic range, which is what makes it dangerous; theophylline and alcohol are first-order at low concentrations and only become zero-order at high ones.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the difference between a loading dose and a maintenance dose?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: The loading dose depends on Vd (fills the volume of distribution); the maintenance dose depends on clearance (replaces what's eliminated). A loading dose bypasses the 4–5 half-life wait for rapid effect.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is therapeutic index (TI), and why does a narrow TI matter?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: TI = ratio of toxic dose to effective dose. Narrow TI = small margin between effective and toxic → needs monitoring. A narrow TI is why digoxin, gentamicin and phenytoin are monitored — and phenytoin is the worst case, because a narrow TI is combined with zero-order kinetics.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which narrow-TI drugs require therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline, gentamicin/vancomycin, warfarin (INR), ciclosporin/tacrolimus.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which drugs are CYP450 inducers, and what is the effect?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: CRAPS: Carbamazepine, Rifampicin, Alcohol (chronic), Phenytoin, Smoking (+ St John's Wort). Effect: ↑enzyme → ↓drug level → reduce efficacy of warfarin, COCP, statins, corticosteroids, ciclosporin. Rifampicin and carbamazepine render the pill ineffective — use alternative contraception.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which drugs are CYP450 inhibitors, and what is the effect?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: ↓enzyme → ↑drug level. Antibiotics: ciprofloxacin, erythromycin/clarithromycin; amiodarone, allopurinol, grapefruit juice (intestinal CYP3A4); isoniazid, omeprazole, sodium valproate; SSRIs — fluoxetine and paroxetine are the potent inhibitors (fluoxetine's effect persists for weeks after stopping), sertraline and citalopram are much weaker; acute alcohol. Effect: ↑toxicity of warfarin, statins, theophylline. Exception — prodrugs: for a drug that needs CYP to become active (clopidogrel, codeine), an inhibitor causes treatment failure, not toxicity. (Allopurinol and valproate belong here by effect, not by enzyme: allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, valproate inhibits glucuronidation.)

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the timing nuance between CYP450 induction and inhibition?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Enzyme induction is delayed (days–weeks — requires new enzyme synthesis); inhibition is rapid (hours). So an inhibitor causes toxicity quickly, an inducer causes failure slowly.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Why do macrolides + statins cause harm?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Macrolides inhibit CYP3A4 → ↑statin levels → myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Check CK if muscle pain develops. Same applies to azole antifungals + statins.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is drug affinity, and how do bond types affect it?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: How well a drug binds to a receptor. Electrostatic = weak + reversible. Covalent = strong + irreversible (aspirin-COX, PPIs-ATPase).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the difference between efficacy and potency?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Efficacy = maximal effect at max dose (Emax). Potency = dose needed to reach EC50. A drug can be highly potent (small dose effective) but low efficacy (small maximum effect).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the difference between selectivity and specificity?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Selectivity = for a specific receptor (bisoprolol = β1-selective; celecoxib = COX-2 selective). Specificity = number of mechanisms (high specificity = one MOA; low = multiple → more side effects).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the agonist spectrum from full agonist to inverse agonist?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Full agonist > partial agonist (submaximal effect even at full occupancy) > antagonist (binds, no effect — blocks agonist) > inverse agonist (binds, produces the opposite effect to the agonist).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are examples of pharmacodynamic drug interactions?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Antagonism: beta-blocker + beta-agonist; naloxone + morphine. Augmentation (↑bleeding): warfarin + NSAIDs, aspirin + clopidogrel. Augmentation (diuretics): furosemide + thiazides → profound hypokalaemia. Serotonin syndrome: SSRIs + tramadol or MDMA or St John's Wort → tremor, limb jerking, hypertonia, dilated pupils, sweating, confusion.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the pharmacokinetic drug interactions by ADME stage?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Absorption: antacids, iron and calcium reduce absorption of tetracyclines, quinolones, bisphosphonates and levothyroxine; prokinetics reduce dwell time; antidiarrhoeal agents increase it. Clopidogrel + omeprazole is not an absorption problem — omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19 and blocks activation of the clopidogrel prodrug (MHRA). Distribution (protein-binding displacement): warfarin displaced by sulfonamides → ↑free warfarin → bleeding, though CYP2C9 inhibition is the dominant mechanism. Metabolism: CYP450 inducers/inhibitors. Elimination: NSAIDs reduce methotrexate excretion (severe toxicity); verapamil and amiodarone raise digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein and reducing digoxin elimination — not by displacement, as digoxin is only about 25% protein bound.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is a Type A (Augmented) ADR?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Exaggeration of normal pharmacological action. Dose-dependent. Primary (intended site): aspirin → bleeding. Secondary (off-target): bisoprolol → bronchospasm.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is a Type B (Bizarre) ADR?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Novel, unexpected response. Often immune-mediated/idiosyncratic. Not dose-dependent. Examples: Reye's syndrome (aspirin), penicillin anaphylaxis, carbamazepine → SJS, G6PD-related haemolysis (e.g. with primaquine, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is a Type C (Continued/Chronic) ADR?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Persists long after stopping. Dose/time-dependent. Corticosteroids → osteoporosis; bisphosphonates → jaw osteonecrosis.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is a Type D (Delayed) ADR?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Appears long after exposure. Examples: carcinogenesis, teratogenicity (thalidomide), tardive dyskinesia (antipsychotics). (Carbimazole → agranulocytosis is instead a Type B/Bizarre idiosyncratic reaction, not Type D.)

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is a Type E (End-of-use/withdrawal) ADR?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Requires tapering not stopping: BZDs (agitation, seizures), corticosteroids (adrenal insufficiency), opioids (flu-like withdrawal), beta-blockers (rebound tachycardia).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the Yellow Card Scheme?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Voluntary reporting of suspected ADRs to the MHRA. Anyone can report — no proof needed. Drugs with ▼ (black triangle) are newly licensed and under intensive monitoring. Particularly important for new drugs and vaccines.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How does steady state relate to route, dose, and loading?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: For a first-order drug, steady state is achieved after 4–5 half-lives regardless of route or dose size — but this does not hold for zero-order drugs such as phenytoin, which have no fixed half-life and take far longer to plateau after a dose change. The loading dose is set by Vd, the maintenance dose by clearance. The loading dose bypasses the wait for rapid effect (digoxin, phenytoin).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What does rifampicin induction reduce, and what harmless effect should patients be warned of?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Rifampicin induction reduces levels of warfarin, COCP, ciclosporin, statins. It turns secretions orange — warn patients (tears, urine, sweat).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How do you distinguish serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Serotonin syndrome = clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis (agitation, tachycardia, hyperthermia). NMS = lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, on antipsychotics.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which drugs should be reviewed, dose-adjusted or withheld when prescribing in significant renal impairment?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Nephrotoxic: gentamicin, vancomycin, NSAIDs, long-term lithium. Renally cleared, so they accumulate: digoxin, lithium, LMWH, metformin, morphine. ACEi/ARB are not directly nephrotoxic — withhold during acute illness or AKI, but do not stop them reflexively in stable proteinuric CKD, where they are renoprotective (NICE).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What do anticoagulants prevent/treat, and how do they differ from antiplatelets?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Anticoagulants prevent/treat thrombosis (VTE — DVT/PE) and arterial thromboembolism, especially AF stroke prevention — distinct from antiplatelets (aspirin/clopidogrel, for arterial/atherosclerotic disease).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which class is now first-line for most anticoagulation indications, and what governs the choice of agent?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: DOACs are now first-line over warfarin for most indications (no routine coagulation monitoring, fewer interactions, no bridging) — warfarin retained for specific situations. The decisive choice is governed by indication, renal function, pregnancy, and the need for reversibility/monitoring.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the target and route of heparins (UFH/LMWH)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Target: activate antithrombin → inactivate thrombin + factor Xa. Route: parenteral (SC/IV).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the target and route of warfarin?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Target: vitamin K antagonist → ↓ factors II, VII, IX, X. Route: oral.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the target and route of DOACs?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Target: direct factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) or direct thrombin inhibitor (dabigatran). Route: oral.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the mechanism of heparins?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Activate antithrombin III → inactivate thrombin + factor Xa.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the key features and uses of LMWH (enoxaparin, dalteparin)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Subcutaneous, predictable, no routine monitoring (anti-Xa levels only in severe renal impairment, extremes of body weight, or pregnancy; monitor platelets for HIT). Uses: VTE prophylaxis — enoxaparin 40 mg SC OD (or dalteparin 5000 units SC OD), a fixed dose; treatment-dose acute VTE — enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg SC OD or 1 mg/kg SC BD on actual body weight; also ACS, bridging, and pregnancy (safe — doesn't cross the placenta).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the renal caution with LMWH?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Renally cleared → below a CrCl of 30 mL/min reduce the treatment dose to enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC once daily (the twice-daily regimen is dropped) and prophylaxis to 20 mg SC once daily; below 15 mL/min use UFH instead.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the uses of UFH (unfractionated heparin) and how is it monitored?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Uses: when rapid on/off is needed (peri-procedure, high bleeding risk), and severe renal impairment. Monitored by APTT, titrated to a ratio of 1.5–2.5 times control (vs LMWH which needs none). Prophylactic dose when LMWH is contraindicated by renal function: 5000 units SC 12-hourly.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the reversal agent and what are the side effects of heparins?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Reversal: protamine sulphate — complete for unfractionated heparin, only PARTIAL for LMWH. Side effects: bleeding, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), osteoporosis (long-term), hyperkalaemia.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and how is it managed?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Immune-mediated platelet drop ~5-10 days in, paradoxically prothrombotic → stop heparin and switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant (NOT LMWH — it cross-reacts). Do not start warfarin until the platelet count recovers (limb gangrene risk), and do not give platelet transfusions.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the mechanism of warfarin?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) → reduces vitamin-K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X (and proteins C & S).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is warfarin monitored, and what are the INR targets?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Monitoring: INR — target 2.5 (range 2–3) for AF and a first DVT/PE; 3.5 for recurrent VTE while therapeutic; 2.5–3.5 for mechanical valves depending on valve type and position. Narrow therapeutic window. Start warfarin 5 mg OD (2–3 mg if elderly, low body weight, liver disease or on an interacting drug), then titrate to INR — maintenance is typically 3–9 mg OD.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Why is warfarin transiently prothrombotic when first started, and what rare skin complication results?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Proteins C & S (anticoagulant) drop first → transient hypercoagulability at initiation. Warfarin also takes several days to work, so in ACUTE VTE cover with LMWH ('bridging') for at least 5 days AND until the INR has been 2 or above for 24 hours (two INRs 24 hours apart), whichever is longer — bridging is NOT routine when starting warfarin for AF. Warfarin-induced skin necrosis is the rare consequence.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which P450 inducers reduce warfarin effect (↓INR)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: P450 inducers (↓warfarin effect → ↓INR): carbamazepine, rifampicin, chronic alcohol, phenytoin, St John's wort.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which P450 inhibitors increase warfarin effect (↑INR → bleeding)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: P450 inhibitors (↑warfarin effect → ↑INR → bleeding): ciprofloxacin, erythromycin/macrolides, acute alcohol, amiodarone, allopurinol, isoniazid, omeprazole, SSRIs, cranberry/grapefruit juice.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is warfarin reversed for a minor/no bleed with a high INR?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: INR 5–8 with no bleeding: withhold 1–2 doses and reduce the maintenance dose — no vitamin K. INR 5–8 with bleeding: stop warfarin, vitamin K 1–3 mg by slow IV injection. INR above 8 with no bleeding: stop warfarin, vitamin K 1–5 mg orally. INR above 8 with bleeding: stop warfarin, vitamin K 1–3 mg by slow IV injection. Repeat at 24 h if still high; restart warfarin when the INR is below 5.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is warfarin reversed in significant bleeding (and if PCC is unavailable)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Significant bleeding: stop warfarin, resuscitate, and give vitamin K (phytomenadione) 5 mg by slow IV injection plus prothrombin complex concentrate 25–50 units/kg IV urgently WITHOUT waiting for the INR result — involve haematology. If PCC is unavailable: FFP 15 mL/kg IV (second-line — slower, less complete, and a large volume load).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: When is warfarin still preferred over DOACs?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Mechanical heart valves, antiphospholipid syndrome, severe renal impairment, moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis. In pregnancy warfarin is contraindicated (teratogenic — warfarin embryopathy) → use LMWH; a mechanical valve is the main exception, managed by specialists.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the two DOAC classes with examples and their reversal agents?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Factor Xa inhibitors ('-xabans'): apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban — andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban (it is not licensed for edoxaban; PCC is used instead). Direct thrombin inhibitor: dabigatran — reverse with idarucizumab.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What advantages make DOACs first-line over warfarin?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Faster onset, fixed dosing, no routine coagulation monitoring (though renal function, FBC and LFTs are checked at baseline and at least annually), fewer food/drug interactions, and no LMWH bridging needed for procedures — the DOAC is simply stopped in advance.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the uses of DOACs?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Non-valvular AF (stroke prevention), VTE treatment + prophylaxis (incl. post-op orthopaedic), increasingly cancer-associated VTE. AF doses: apixaban 5 mg BD (2.5 mg BD if CrCl 15–29, or if two of: age 80+, weight 60 kg or under, creatinine 133 micromol/L or more); rivaroxaban 20 mg OD with food (15 mg OD if CrCl 15–49); edoxaban 60 mg OD (30 mg OD if CrCl 15–50, weight 60 kg or under, or on a P-gp inhibitor); dabigatran 150 mg BD (110 mg BD if 80 or over, or on verapamil). VTE treatment: apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD; rivaroxaban 15 mg BD for 21 days then 20 mg OD; edoxaban and dabigatran only after at least 5 days of a parenteral anticoagulant.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the cautions/contraindications of DOACs?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Renal impairment (apixaban avoided when CrCl <15 mL/min [caution 15–29]; rivaroxaban avoided <15); contraindicated in pregnancy/breastfeeding (use LMWH); dabigatran ↑dyspepsia/GI bleeding; NOT for mechanical valves or antiphospholipid syndrome.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which DOAC tends to have the most favourable bleeding profile?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Apixaban tends to have the most favourable bleeding profile (especially GI).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the preferred agent for non-valvular AF / most VTE, and for a mechanical heart valve?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Non-valvular AF / most VTE: DOAC (first-line). Mechanical heart valve: warfarin (DOACs contraindicated).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the preferred agent for antiphospholipid syndrome and for pregnancy?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Antiphospholipid syndrome: warfarin. Pregnancy: LMWH (warfarin teratogenic, DOACs unsafe).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the preferred agent for severe renal impairment and for inpatient VTE prophylaxis?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Severe renal impairment: warfarin or UFH (apixaban is the DOAC least affected but is still avoided below a CrCl of 15 mL/min). Inpatient VTE prophylaxis: LMWH.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the preferred agent when rapid on/off is needed (peri-op, high bleed risk)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: UFH (short half-life, APTT-monitored).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the major complication of anticoagulation, and how is it balanced in AF?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Major complication = bleeding (GI, intracranial). In AF, balance bleeding risk (ORBIT, which NICE now specifies, or the older HAS-BLED) against CHA₂DS₂-VASc (thrombotic/stroke risk) — and a high bleeding score prompts you to modify reversible risk factors, NOT to withhold anticoagulation.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the reversal agents for heparin/LMWH and for warfarin?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Heparin / LMWH: protamine sulphate (complete for UFH, only partial for LMWH). Warfarin: vitamin K 5 mg IV + prothrombin complex concentrate 25–50 units/kg for major bleeding.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the reversal agents for dabigatran and for apixaban/rivaroxaban?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Dabigatran: idarucizumab. Apixaban / rivaroxaban: andexanet alfa (or PCC) — andexanet alfa is not licensed for edoxaban, for which PCC is used.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is palliative care (WHO definition)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Holistic care focused on quality of life in life-limiting illness — physical, psychological, social, spiritual. Not just end-of-life — it can run alongside active treatment.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Who makes up the palliative care MDT?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Palliative care nurses (Macmillan / Marie Curie), specialist palliative teams, hospice, community services.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is anticipatory ('just in case') prescribing, and what are the four core end-of-life medications? (highest-yield)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Four core end-of-life medications prescribed in advance as PRN subcutaneous injections (a syringe driver is not prescribed in anticipation — it is started only when symptoms recur): opioid — morphine 2.5–5 mg SC PRN, minimum 1-hourly; antiemetic — haloperidol 500 micrograms–1.5 mg SC PRN 4-hourly, or levomepromazine 2.5–6.25 mg SC PRN; antisecretory — hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg, hyoscine hydrobromide 400 micrograms, or glycopyrronium 200 micrograms SC PRN (secretions/'death rattle'); sedative — midazolam 2.5–5 mg SC PRN, minimum 1-hourly. Note the units: the two hyoscines sit on the same chart at 20 mg and 400 micrograms.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What does advance care planning (DNACPR / ReSPECT) involve?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Document wishes, preferred place of care/death, and resuscitation status early.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the three steps of the WHO analgesic ladder in palliative care?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: 1 — Non-opioid ± adjuvant (paracetamol 1 g QDS, max 4 g/24 h; NSAID). 2 — Weak opioid + non-opioid ± adjuvant (codeine 30–60 mg QDS, max 240 mg/24 h; dihydrocodeine 30 mg 4–6-hourly). 3 — Strong opioid + non-opioid ± adjuvant (morphine, oxycodone). Adjuvants at every step (amitriptyline/gabapentin/pregabalin for neuropathic pain, steroids, bisphosphonates).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is the breakthrough morphine dose calculated? (high-yield)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: In the opioid-naive, start oral morphine 20–30 mg/24 h — modified-release 10–15 mg BD, or immediate-release 5 mg 4-hourly (2.5 mg if frail, elderly or renally impaired) — with immediate-release morphine 5 mg PRN for breakthrough (NICE). Breakthrough dose = total 24-hour opioid dose ÷ 6. E.g. morphine 30mg BD → breakthrough = (60)÷6 = 10mg. If not controlled, either increase the regular 24-hour dose by 30–50%, or add the total breakthrough consumed in the previous 24h to the regular dose. Recalculate the breakthrough dose (still one sixth of the new 24-hour total) every time the regular dose changes.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is morphine dosing adjusted for renal impairment?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: In mild-moderate renal impairment switch to oxycodone (morphine's active metabolites accumulate). In severe renal impairment (eGFR under 30) oxycodone also accumulates — alfentanil or fentanyl is preferred, at reduced doses.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How do you convert opioid doses (oral to SC, and between opioids)? (high-yield)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Ratios are drug-specific — never carry one across to a different opioid. Oral morphine → SC morphine: divide the total 24-hour dose by 2. Oral morphine → SC diamorphine: divide by 3. Oral morphine → oral oxycodone: divide by 2. Codeine → oral morphine: divide by 10. When rotating between opioids, reduce the calculated dose by 25–50% for incomplete cross-tolerance and reassess within 24 hours.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the signs of opioid toxicity, and how is it managed?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Signs: drowsiness, confusion, myoclonus, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression. Action: reduce dose / rotate opioid + ensure hydration. Naloxone only if life-threatening respiratory depression — dilute 400 micrograms to 10 mL and give 20–100 microgram boluses every 1–2 minutes, titrated against respiratory rate, not consciousness. This is deliberately unlike the resuscitation approach of giving the whole 400-microgram ampoule as one bolus, which reverses analgesia entirely and precipitates severe pain and withdrawal.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is breathlessness managed in palliative care?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Low-dose opioids — morphine 2.5 mg orally 4-hourly PRN, or 2.5 mg SC PRN, in the opioid-naive (roughly half the analgesic starting dose), titrated to effect; if already on morphine for pain, use the existing breakthrough dose — ± benzodiazepine for the anxiety component. Non-drug measures: handheld fan, positioning, reassurance. Treat reversible causes (effusion, anaemia).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Why must a laxative always be co-prescribed with opioids in palliation? (key prescribing-safety point)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Constipation is near-universal with opioids → ALWAYS co-prescribe a laxative, unless there is bowel obstruction or diarrhoea: stimulant (senna 15 mg at night, increased to 30 mg if needed) ± softener/osmotic (macrogol 1 sachet daily, up to 3 in divided doses, or docusate). Avoid bulk-forming laxatives in the dying patient.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is agitation / terminal restlessness managed?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Midazolam 2.5–5 mg SC PRN, minimum 1-hourly, first-line; convert to a syringe driver if 2–3 PRN doses are needed in 24 h. Haloperidol or levomepromazine as alternatives. Exclude reversible causes (urinary retention, pain, constipation).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is hyoscine hydrobromide used for in palliation?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: A muscarinic antagonist that crosses the BBB (also sedating/antiemetic) — used for respiratory secretions ('death rattle'), 400 micrograms SC PRN (max 2.4 mg/24 h). Hyoscine butylbromide and glycopyrronium are equally effective and do not cross the BBB. Bowel colic is treated with hyoscine BUTYLbromide (Buscopan) 20 mg SC PRN, max 120 mg/24 h — note that the two hyoscines are dosed in different units.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the antiemetics for palliation by cause? (high-yield)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Intracranial causes: cyclizine 50 mg up to TDS, 1st line (H1 receptor antagonist — acts on vomiting centre). GI dysmotility: metoclopramide 10 mg up to TDS (D2 antagonist — prokinetic; max 5 days — MHRA), but avoid in complete bowel obstruction or colic. Chemical/metabolic (uraemia, hypercalcaemia, opioid-induced): haloperidol 500 micrograms–1.5 mg (D2 antagonist at the chemoreceptor trigger zone). Refractory or multifactorial: levomepromazine. Chemo-/radiotherapy-induced: ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist) — not a general palliative antiemetic, as it worsens opioid constipation.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is raised ICP headache managed in palliation?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Dexamethasone 8–16 mg daily initially, then tapered every 3–7 days to the minimum effective dose — reduces peritumoural oedema in brain mets/primary brain tumour. Give as a single morning dose to avoid insomnia, co-prescribe gastroprotection (omeprazole 20 mg OD), and monitor blood glucose.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is metastatic bone pain managed?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Analgesics (WHO pain ladder) + bisphosphonates (zoledronate — reduces skeletal events) + radiotherapy (single fraction for bone mets). Pathological fracture: orthopaedic surgery then radiotherapy.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How are persistent hiccups managed in palliation?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Chlorpromazine or haloperidol — both D2 antagonists. Baclofen (GABA agonist) as alternative. Persistent hiccups in the palliative context are often due to gastric distension, uraemia, or diaphragmatic irritation.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the features of the intravenous (IV) route?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: 100% bioavailability. Fastest onset (5–10 min). Not affected by first-pass metabolism. Risk: infection, phlebitis, air embolism. Volume: theoretically unlimited but practically titrated.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the features of the intramuscular (IM) route?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: High but variable bioavailability (only IV is 100% by definition — absorption falls in shock or poor perfusion). Max volume 5ml. Contraindicated in haemophilia (risk of massive haematoma). Examples: adrenaline, glucagon, vaccines.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the features of the subcutaneous (SC) route?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: High but variable bioavailability (only IV is 100% by definition). Max volume 2ml. Slower absorption than IM. Used in syringe drivers (palliation), insulin, LMWH, GLP-1 agonists.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the features of the buccal/sublingual (SL) route?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Bypasses first-pass metabolism. Fast absorption. Examples: GTN (angina), buprenorphine, midazolam (seizures). Oral = variable bioavailability (hepatic first-pass reduces drug availability by up to 90% for some drugs).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the features of the inhaled (INH) route?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Local effects: SABA, ICS, ipratropium. Systemic effects: volatile anaesthetics. Drugs modified to reduce systemic absorption (e.g. poorly soluble ICS in lung).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the features of the topical/transdermal (TOP) route?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Local: creams, ointments. Systemic delivery if highly lipid-soluble: nicotine patches, fentanyl patches (palliative), oestrogen patches, GTN patch. Bypasses first-pass. Fentanyl patches are not for opioid-naive patients or unstable pain — they take 12–24h to work, a depot persists after removal, absorption rises with fever or external heat, and breakthrough opioid must still be prescribed.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the features of the epidural/intrathecal (EP) route?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Epidural: outside the dura — used for analgesia/anaesthesia; SEs — dural puncture headache, abscess, haematoma, hypotension. Intrathecal: within the subarachnoid space — used for analgesia and intrathecal chemotherapy.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the features of the rectal/vaginal (PR) route?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Rectal: relatively rapid but variable absorption, and partially bypasses first-pass metabolism — useful when the oral route is lost. Vaginal: usually used for local effect, though systemic absorption occurs and first-pass is avoided. Examples: diazepam PR (seizures), misoprostol PV, progesterone PV.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the NICE daily fluid requirements?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Water: 25–30 mL/kg/day. Electrolytes: 1 mmol/kg/day of Na, K, and Cl. Glucose: 50–100 g/day (caloric requirement). Typical 70kg adult: 500mL 0.9% saline (+20mmol K⁺) + 1500mL 5% dextrose (+40mmol K⁺) over 24h (≈2L ≈ 28 mL/kg).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the signs of hypovolaemia and the resuscitation fluid approach?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Signs: BP <100/60, HR >90, cap refill >2s, RR >20, decreased O₂ sats, ↓urine output. Fluid challenge: 500ml crystalloid STAT (15 mins). Reduce to 250ml in elderly/HF/CKD. Repeat up to 2000ml then seek senior review.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the difference between crystalloids and colloids for resuscitation?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Crystalloids: normal saline, Hartmann's (balanced — preferred to avoid hyperchloraemic acidosis). Colloids (albumin): remain intravascular longer but risk of anaphylaxis — rarely used.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the rules for potassium (K⁺) administration? (high-yield)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Never give K⁺ faster than 20 mmol/hour (risk of fatal cardiac arrhythmia). Peripheral line: max 40 mmol/L concentration (causes thrombophlebitis if higher). Central line: can give more concentrated K⁺ with continuous cardiac monitoring. Never give K⁺ as a bolus.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the framework for analgesic prescribing?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Assess the pain → classify it → treat by the WHO ladder + by mechanism → prescribe opioids safely.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the two key pain classifications, and their clinical relevance?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Acute vs chronic (chronic = >3 months). Nociceptive vs neuropathic (different drugs — opioids work poorly on neuropathic pain).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is pain assessed, given it is subjective?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Pain is subjective — measured by the patient's report: Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Numerical Rating Scale (NRS, 0–10). SOCRATES for characterising pain; DN4 questionnaire (≥4/10 → neuropathic). Assess impact (function, sleep, mood) — pain is biopsychosocial.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the features of nociceptive pain, and what does it respond to?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Mechanism: tissue damage → nociceptor activation. Character: aching, throbbing, well-localised. Responds to: the WHO ladder (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the features of neuropathic pain, and what does it respond to?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Mechanism: nerve damage/dysfunction. Character: burning, shooting, tingling, allodynia. Responds to: neuropathic agents (opioids work poorly).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How do you treat acute vs chronic pain by type?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Acute (recent, protective, self-limiting): treat the cause + WHO ladder. Chronic (>3 months): multimodal; chronic primary pain → avoid most analgesia.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the three steps of the WHO analgesic ladder?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Step 1 (mild): non-opioid — paracetamol 1 g QDS (max 4 g/24 h) ± NSAID (ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food, max 2.4 g/24 h; or naproxen 250–500 mg BD with food, max 1 g/24 h) (± adjuvant). Step 2 (moderate): weak opioid — codeine 30–60 mg 4-hourly PRN (max 240 mg/24 h), dihydrocodeine 30 mg 4–6-hourly PRN (max 180 mg/24 h), or tramadol 50–100 mg 4–6-hourly PRN (max 400 mg/24 h) (+ non-opioid ± adjuvant). Step 3 (severe): strong opioid — in the opioid-naive, modified-release morphine 10 mg BD (or immediate-release 5 mg 4-hourly) with immediate-release morphine 5 mg PRN for breakthrough (+ non-opioid ± adjuvant). Originally for cancer pain.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the principles of the WHO ladder ('by the mouth, by the clock, by the ladder, for the individual')?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Oral route preferred, regular dosing (not just PRN) for continuous pain, step-wise, individualised. Leapfrogging allowed — severe pain → start at Step 3 directly; breakthrough pain → a fast-acting rescue dose of immediate-release morphine, one sixth of the total 24-hour oral morphine dose (so 5 mg if the total is 30 mg/24 h).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is Step 4 (the modern addition) of the WHO ladder?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Interventional — nerve blocks, spinal analgesia, spinal cord stimulation.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the opioid-crisis caveat regarding the WHO ladder?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: The ladder drove opioid overuse in chronic non-cancer pain; weak opioids (Step 2) add little and modern practice questions them.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the mechanism and key caution of paracetamol?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Central mechanism (poorly understood). Hepatotoxic in overdose. Adult dose paracetamol 1 g QDS, maximum 4 g/24 h; dose-reduce in liver disease and at low body weight — if under 50 kg, reduce to 500 mg every 4–6 hours.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the mechanism and key cautions of NSAIDs?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Inhibit COX → ↓prostaglandins. Cautions: GI ulcer/bleed, renal impairment, CVD, asthma; avoid in CKD/PUD/heart failure. Co-prescribe a PPI (omeprazole 20 mg OD, or lansoprazole 30 mg OD) for as long as the NSAID continues, and use the lowest effective dose for the shortest period — ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food (max 2.4 g/24 h) or naproxen 250–500 mg BD with food (max 1 g/24 h).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the mechanism and key cautions of weak opioids (codeine, tramadol)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: µ-opioid agonist; codeine is a prodrug → morphine (CYP2D6). Codeine is ineffective in poor metabolisers, dangerous in ultra-rapid metabolisers — hence contraindicated under 12 years, in breastfeeding, and in under-18s after tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy for sleep apnoea (MHRA); tramadol 50–100 mg 4–6-hourly PRN (max 400 mg/24 h) also lowers the seizure threshold + is serotonergic.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the mechanism of strong opioids (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl)?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: µ-opioid agonist.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What must ALWAYS be co-prescribed with opioids, and why?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: ALWAYS co-prescribe a laxative — senna 15 mg at night (± docusate 100 mg BD if stools are hard) — because constipation is near-universal. Consider a PRN antiemetic when starting: metoclopramide 10 mg up to TDS (max 5 days — MHRA) or cyclizine 50 mg up to TDS.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the side effects of opioids?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Constipation (near-universal), nausea (often transient), drowsiness (mild sedation on starting or increasing a dose is expected and usually settles within a few days — persistent or worsening drowsiness with confusion is toxicity), respiratory depression, pruritus, tolerance + dependence.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the features of opioid toxicity, and when is naloxone used?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Drowsiness → confusion, pinpoint pupils, myoclonus, respiratory depression → reduce dose / rotate opioid. Naloxone only if respiratory depression is life-threatening — unrousable, or respiratory rate under 8 — 400 micrograms IV, repeated every 2–3 minutes to a maximum of 10 mg. In a patient taking opioids for pain, dilute 400 micrograms to 10 mL and give 100-microgram boluses, titrating to respiratory rate rather than conscious level.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: Which opioids are preferred in renal impairment, and why?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Morphine accumulates (active metabolites) → use oxycodone (still at a reduced dose), or fentanyl/buprenorphine, in renal impairment.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is patient-controlled analgesia (PCA), and its key safety points?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: IV strong opioid, patient-triggered, locked to prevent overdose; needs anaesthetic input + naloxone/antiemetic/atropine available; avoid other PRN opioids alongside.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are opioid patches used for?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Buprenorphine, fentanyl — for stable chronic pain, not acute titration (background analgesia). Never start a fentanyl patch in an opioid-naive patient, and warn that heat — fever, a hot bath, a heat pad — increases absorption (MHRA).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What is the NICE first-line for neuropathic pain?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Opioids work poorly — use specific agents. NICE first-line (choose one of four): amitriptyline 10 mg at night, increased in 10 mg steps to 25–75 mg at night; duloxetine 60 mg OD; gabapentin 300 mg OD increasing over 3 days to TDS, then in 300 mg steps to a maximum of 3.6 g/24 h; or pregabalin 75 mg BD, increased to a maximum of 600 mg/24 h. Switch if one fails. Gabapentin and pregabalin are Schedule 3 controlled drugs — dependence and misuse potential.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the additional options and causes for neuropathic pain?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Tramadol as rescue only; capsaicin cream for localised; carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia specifically — 100 mg once or twice daily, increased in 100–200 mg steps until the pain is controlled. Causes: diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, nerve impingement, MS, trigeminal neuralgia.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the adjuvant analgesic classes and their uses?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Antidepressants (amitriptyline, duloxetine — neuropathic); anticonvulsants (gabapentin/pregabalin — neuropathic; both Schedule 3 controlled drugs); corticosteroids (inflammatory/nerve compression/raised ICP); bisphosphonates (metastatic bone pain); benzodiazepines (muscle spasm), antispasmodics.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How does NICE recommend managing chronic primary pain (e.g. fibromyalgia)? (high-yield SBA)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Chronic primary pain (no underlying cause): NICE recommends avoiding most analgesia (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids/gabapentinoids) → instead exercise, psychological therapy (CBT/ACT), and consider an antidepressant (e.g. duloxetine or amitriptyline).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is chronic secondary pain (with an underlying cause) managed?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Treat the cause + multimodal analgesia. Multimodal/biopsychosocial: physiotherapy, psychology, pain clinic; minimise long-term opioids (limited benefit + harms in chronic non-cancer pain).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is post-operative pain managed?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Regular paracetamol + NSAID + PRN IMMEDIATE-RELEASE opioid — modified-release opioids are NOT used for acute post-operative pain (they cannot be titrated against a rapidly falling requirement, they accumulate in the opioid-naive, and they drive persistent post-surgical opioid use); local anaesthetic wound infiltration; PCA; step the opioid down daily as the patient recovers.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: How is acute severe pain managed?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Titrated IV opioid — morphine 1–2 mg IV repeated every 5 minutes, titrated to pain and respiratory rate.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What are the two organising principles for drugs to avoid in pregnancy?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Timing matters: the 1st trimester (organogenesis) is most vulnerable to structural malformations; some drugs (ACEi, NSAIDs) harm specifically in the 2nd/3rd trimester. Always ask 'could she be pregnant?' before prescribing in any woman of childbearing age, and switch teratogenic drugs pre-conception where possible.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What fetal harm does warfarin cause, and what is the safe alternative?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Warfarin embryopathy — nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses, limb hypoplasia; CNS defects; haemorrhage/fetal loss. Safe alternative: LMWH (doesn't cross the placenta).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What fetal harm do ACE inhibitors / ARBs cause, and what are the safe alternatives?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: 2nd/3rd trimester: oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure/anuria, skull hypoplasia, lung hypoplasia. Safe alternatives: labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What fetal harm does sodium valproate cause, and what are the safe alternatives?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Neural tube defects (spina bifida), fetal valproate syndrome, developmental delay — the highest-risk AED. Valproate must not be used in any woman or girl able to have children unless the conditions of the Pregnancy Prevention Programme are met, and must not be started in any new patient under 55, male or female, unless two specialists independently document that there is no alternative (MHRA). Preferred alternatives: lamotrigine or levetiracetam — lowest risk, but not risk-free (lamotrigine levels fall in pregnancy and need monitoring).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What harm do other AEDs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, topiramate) cause, and what are the alternatives?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: NTDs, cleft lip/palate, fetal hydantoin syndrome. Topiramate has its own Pregnancy Prevention Programme (MHRA) — cleft lip/palate, low birth weight and a possible risk of intellectual disability, autism and ADHD. Alternatives: lamotrigine/levetiracetam, with folic acid 5 mg daily from before conception until 12 weeks.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What fetal harm does lithium cause, and how is it managed?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Ebstein's anomaly (tricuspid valve defect) — a real but small absolute risk, about 1–2 per 1,000 with 1st-trimester exposure. Needs specialist review; do not stop lithium abruptly, as the relapse risk may outweigh the fetal risk.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What harm does methotrexate cause, and what is the pre-conception advice?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Abortifacient, multiple malformations. Stop before conception — at least 3 months conventionally, though UK rheumatology guidance supports 1 month in women and 3 months in men.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What fetal harm does isotretinoin (retinoids) cause, and what programme is required?
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.back: Severe CNS/cardiac/craniofacial defects → requires a strict pregnancy-prevention programme.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.front: What fetal harm do tetracyclines (e.g. doxycycline) cause, and what are the safe alternatives?
