Also avoid nephrotoxic/hepatotoxic drugs where an alternative exists, monitor organ function and drug levels, and review the whole drug chart.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the bioavailability of an intravenously administered drug, and why?
options: Variable, depending on gut pH
50%, due to first-pass metabolism
Reduced by up to 90% by hepatic metabolism
100% by definition, because it bypasses absorption and first-pass metabolism
Dependent on transit time
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: 100% by definition, because it bypasses absorption and first-pass metabolism
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Bioavailability (F) = AUC(oral)/AUC(IV), and IV = 100% by definition because it reaches the systemic circulation directly, bypassing absorption and first-pass metabolism.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following, given by the stated route, undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism and so has low bioavailability?
options: Oral morphine, oral propranolol and oral TCAs
IV adrenaline
Sublingual GTN
Buccal buprenorphine
Inhaled salbutamol
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Oral morphine, oral propranolol and oral TCAs
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Oral morphine, propranolol and TCAs undergo high first-pass metabolism (gut wall + liver), giving low oral bioavailability. Sublingual and buccal routes (GTN, buprenorphine) bypass first-pass metabolism entirely — which is exactly why GTN is given sublingually. Note that isosorbide mononitrate is the exception among nitrates: it has ~100% oral bioavailability.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A highly protein-bound drug such as warfarin or heparin has which volume of distribution characteristic?
options: A high Vd, distributing widely into tissues
An unmeasurable Vd
A low Vd, remaining largely in the plasma
A Vd equal to total body water
A Vd of zero
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: A low Vd, remaining largely in the plasma
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Highly protein-bound drugs (heparin, warfarin) have a low Vd and stay in the plasma. Drugs with a high Vd (amiodarone, chloroquine, digoxin) distribute widely into tissues.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A drug is eliminated at a constant amount per unit time regardless of concentration because its metabolic pathway is saturated. What kinetics is this, and which drugs follow it?
options: First-order kinetics; a constant fraction is eliminated, as for most drugs
Zero-order kinetics; but only for drugs given by the intravenous route
First-order kinetics; phenytoin, salicylates, theophylline and alcohol
Saturation-independent kinetics; the rate is fixed by renal clearance alone
Zero-order kinetics; phenytoin, aspirin/salicylates (high dose), theophylline, alcohol (PASTA)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Zero-order kinetics; phenytoin, aspirin/salicylates (high dose), theophylline, alcohol (PASTA)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Zero-order kinetics means a constant amount is eliminated per unit time (the pathway is saturated). The drugs are remembered by PASTA: Phenytoin, Aspirin/Salicylates (high dose — A and S are the same agent), Theophylline, Alcohol. Once saturated, a small dose increase causes a disproportionately large rise in concentration → toxicity. Phenytoin saturates within the therapeutic range, which is what makes it dangerous.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Approximately how many half-lives are needed for a drug with first-order kinetics to reach steady state?
options: 1 half-life
4–5 half-lives
10 half-lives
Steady state is never reached
Immediately, regardless of dose
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: 4–5 half-lives
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: A first-order drug reaches steady state after 4–5 half-lives (5 half-lives leaves <5% of the drug), regardless of route or dose size. This does not hold for zero-order drugs such as phenytoin, which have no fixed half-life and take far longer to plateau after a dose change.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What determines the loading dose versus the maintenance dose of a drug?
options: The loading dose depends on clearance (replaces what is eliminated); the maintenance dose depends on Vd (fills the volume of distribution)
Both depend on bioavailability alone, so neither changes with renal or hepatic impairment
Both depend on half-life alone, so both are unchanged if the volume of distribution changes
The loading dose depends on Vd (fills the volume of distribution); the maintenance dose depends on clearance (replaces what is eliminated)
Neither depends on pharmacokinetics — both are set empirically by the licensed dose range
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: The loading dose depends on Vd (fills the volume of distribution); the maintenance dose depends on clearance (replaces what is eliminated)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The loading dose depends on Vd (it fills the volume of distribution) and bypasses the 4–5 half-life wait for rapid effect; the maintenance dose depends on clearance (replacing what is eliminated). Examples include digoxin and phenytoin.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following drugs has a narrow therapeutic index requiring therapeutic drug monitoring?
options: Digoxin
Paracetamol
Amoxicillin
Cetirizine
Omeprazole
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Digoxin
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Narrow-TI drugs requiring TDM include digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline, gentamicin/vancomycin, warfarin (INR), and ciclosporin/tacrolimus. A narrow TI means a small margin between effective and toxic doses.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on warfarin is started on rifampicin. What happens to the warfarin effect, and by what mechanism?
options: Warfarin effect increases due to enzyme inhibition
No interaction occurs
Warfarin effect decreases because rifampicin is a CYP450 inducer, reducing warfarin levels
Warfarin is displaced from protein
Rifampicin blocks warfarin absorption
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Warfarin effect decreases because rifampicin is a CYP450 inducer, reducing warfarin levels
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Rifampicin is a CYP450 inducer (CRAPS: Carbamazepine, Rifampicin, Alcohol chronic, Phenytoin, Smoking). Induction increases enzyme activity → reduced drug levels, so warfarin (and COCP, ciclosporin, statins) efficacy falls. Rifampicin also turns secretions orange.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A woman on the combined oral contraceptive pill is prescribed rifampicin. What advice is correct?
options: The pill remains fully effective, as rifampicin does not affect hormonal contraception
The pill dose should be halved, since rifampicin raises circulating oestrogen levels
Rifampicin increases the pill's effect, so the risk is of oestrogen-related side effects
No action is required, provided the rifampicin course lasts less than two weeks
Rifampicin (an enzyme inducer) renders the pill ineffective, so alternative contraception is needed
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Rifampicin (an enzyme inducer) renders the pill ineffective, so alternative contraception is needed
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Rifampicin and carbamazepine are enzyme inducers that render the combined oral contraceptive pill ineffective by lowering hormone levels — alternative contraception should be used.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on a statin is prescribed clarithromycin (a macrolide) and develops muscle pain. What is the mechanism, and what should be checked?
options: The macrolide induces CYP3A4, lowering statin levels; check LFTs
The macrolide inhibits CYP3A4, raising statin levels and risking myopathy/rhabdomyolysis; check CK
The statin displaces the macrolide from protein; check INR
The macrolide reduces statin absorption; no check needed
There is no interaction
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: The macrolide inhibits CYP3A4, raising statin levels and risking myopathy/rhabdomyolysis; check CK
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Macrolides inhibit CYP3A4 → increased statin levels → myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Check CK if muscle pain develops. The same applies to azole antifungals + statins.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Why does a CYP450 inhibitor cause toxicity quickly, whereas an inducer causes treatment failure slowly?
options: Inhibition requires new enzyme synthesis; induction is immediate
Both act instantly
Inducers act within minutes
Inhibition is rapid (hours); induction is delayed (days–weeks) because it requires new enzyme synthesis
There is no difference in timing
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Inhibition is rapid (hours); induction is delayed (days–weeks) because it requires new enzyme synthesis
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Enzyme inhibition is rapid (hours), so an inhibitor causes toxicity quickly. Enzyme induction is delayed (days–weeks) because it requires new enzyme synthesis, so an inducer causes failure slowly.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A drug requires only a very small dose to be effective but produces a small maximum effect. How is this best described?
options: High potency, low efficacy
High efficacy, low potency
High efficacy and high potency
Low potency and low efficacy
It is an antagonist
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: High potency, low efficacy
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Potency is the dose needed to reach EC50, and efficacy is the maximal effect (Emax). A drug that is effective at a small dose but has a small maximum effect is highly potent but of low efficacy.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which term describes a drug that binds to a receptor but produces the opposite effect to the natural agonist?
options: Partial agonist
Antagonist
Inverse agonist
Full agonist
Allosteric modulator
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Inverse agonist
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The agonist spectrum runs: full agonist > partial agonist (submaximal effect even at full occupancy) > antagonist (binds, no effect, blocks the agonist) > inverse agonist (binds and produces the opposite effect to the agonist).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on warfarin is co-prescribed a sulfonamide antibiotic and begins bleeding. Which pharmacokinetic interaction mechanism explains this?
options: Reduced absorption of warfarin from the gut, lowering the amount that reaches the circulation
Increased warfarin metabolism by enzyme induction, raising the INR through faster clearance
Increased renal clearance of warfarin, leaving less drug available to be protein bound
Antagonism at the vitamin K epoxide reductase receptor, which is a pharmacodynamic mechanism
Protein-binding displacement — the sulfonamide displaces warfarin, increasing free warfarin and causing bleeding
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Protein-binding displacement — the sulfonamide displaces warfarin, increasing free warfarin and causing bleeding
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: This is classically taught as a distribution (protein-binding displacement) interaction: warfarin is displaced by sulfonamides → increased free warfarin → bleeding. In reality CYP2C9 inhibition of warfarin metabolism by the sulfonamide is the dominant mechanism, with displacement contributing — either way the INR rises, and the interaction is pharmacokinetic rather than pharmacodynamic. (Quinidine, verapamil and amiodarone raise digoxin levels by a different route again — they inhibit P-glycoprotein and reduce digoxin elimination, not by displacement.)

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on methotrexate is given an NSAID and develops severe toxicity. Which pharmacokinetic mechanism is responsible?
options: The NSAID induces methotrexate metabolism
The NSAID reduces methotrexate excretion (elimination interaction), causing severe toxicity
The NSAID displaces methotrexate from protein
The NSAID blocks methotrexate absorption
There is no interaction
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: The NSAID reduces methotrexate excretion (elimination interaction), causing severe toxicity
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: NSAIDs reduce methotrexate excretion (an elimination interaction), causing severe toxicity. Similarly, verapamil/quinidine/amiodarone reduce digoxin excretion.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on an SSRI is given tramadol and develops tremor, limb jerking, hypertonia, dilated pupils and confusion. What is this interaction?
options: An antagonistic pharmacodynamic interaction between the two drugs
A protein-binding displacement interaction raising the free drug level
An absorption interaction reducing the bioavailability of one drug
Serotonin syndrome — a pharmacodynamic interaction from combined serotonergic drugs
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome from dopamine blockade by an antipsychotic
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Serotonin syndrome — a pharmacodynamic interaction from combined serotonergic drugs
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Serotonin syndrome is a pharmacodynamic interaction: SSRIs + tramadol (or MDMA or St John's Wort) → tremor, limb jerking, hypertonia, dilated pupils, sweating and confusion.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient develops penicillin anaphylaxis — a novel, unpredictable, immune-mediated, non-dose-dependent reaction. Which type of ADR is this?
options: Type B (Bizarre)
Type A (Augmented)
Type C (Continued)
Type D (Delayed)
Type E (End-of-use)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Type B (Bizarre)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type B (Bizarre) ADRs are novel, unexpected, often immune-mediated/idiosyncratic and not dose-dependent — e.g. penicillin anaphylaxis, Reye's syndrome, carbamazepine → SJS, and G6PD-related haemolysis.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following requires tapering rather than abrupt stopping?
options: A single dose of paracetamol taken for a headache
A one-off five-day antibiotic course for a chest infection
Long-term corticosteroids (risk of adrenal insufficiency), benzodiazepines, opioids, and beta-blockers
Topical emollients applied for dry skin
An inhaled short-acting beta agonist used as required
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Long-term corticosteroids (risk of adrenal insufficiency), benzodiazepines, opioids, and beta-blockers
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type E (End-of-use/withdrawal) ADRs require tapering not stopping: benzodiazepines (agitation, seizures), corticosteroids (adrenal insufficiency), opioids (flu-like withdrawal), and beta-blockers (rebound tachycardia).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How can serotonin syndrome be distinguished from neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)?
options: Serotonin syndrome causes lead-pipe rigidity; NMS causes clonus
They are clinically identical
NMS causes hyperreflexia; serotonin syndrome causes rigidity
Serotonin syndrome only occurs with antipsychotics
Serotonin syndrome = clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis; NMS = lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, on antipsychotics
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Serotonin syndrome = clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis; NMS = lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, on antipsychotics
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Serotonin syndrome features clonus, hyperreflexia and mydriasis (with agitation, tachycardia, hyperthermia), whereas NMS features lead-pipe rigidity and bradyreflexia and occurs on antipsychotics.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following drugs should be reviewed, dose-adjusted or withheld when prescribing in significant renal impairment?
options: Paracetamol and inhaled salbutamol
Gentamicin, vancomycin, NSAIDs, ACEi, digoxin, lithium, LMWH, metformin, and morphine
Inhaled corticosteroids only
Topical emollients
None require review
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Gentamicin, vancomycin, NSAIDs, ACEi, digoxin, lithium, LMWH, metformin, and morphine
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: In significant renal impairment, review both nephrotoxic and renally-cleared drugs. Nephrotoxic: gentamicin, vancomycin, NSAIDs, long-term lithium. Renally cleared, so they accumulate: digoxin, lithium, LMWH, metformin, morphine. ACEi/ARB are not directly nephrotoxic — withhold during acute illness or AKI, but do not stop them reflexively in stable proteinuric CKD.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How do anticoagulants differ from antiplatelets in their primary role?
options: Anticoagulants treat arterial/atherosclerotic disease; antiplatelets treat venous thrombosis
They are interchangeable in all indications, so either class may be used for any thrombotic problem
Anticoagulants are used only in pregnancy, where antiplatelets are contraindicated
Anticoagulants prevent and treat thrombosis (VTE and AF stroke prevention); antiplatelets target arterial atherosclerotic disease
Antiplatelets are first-line for AF stroke prevention
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Anticoagulants prevent and treat thrombosis (VTE and AF stroke prevention); antiplatelets target arterial atherosclerotic disease
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Anticoagulants prevent/treat thrombosis (VTE — DVT/PE) and arterial thromboembolism, especially AF stroke prevention; this is distinct from antiplatelets (aspirin/clopidogrel) used for arterial/atherosclerotic disease.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Why are DOACs the modern first-line over warfarin for most indications?
options: They need no routine coagulation monitoring, have fewer interactions, and need no bridging
They require frequent INR monitoring with dose adjustment at every clinic visit
They are safe in mechanical heart valves, unlike warfarin which is now avoided there
They are preferred in pregnancy
They have a narrower therapeutic window
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: They need no routine coagulation monitoring, have fewer interactions, and need no bridging
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: DOACs are first-line over warfarin for most indications because they need no routine coagulation monitoring, have fewer interactions and need no bridging — though renal function must still be checked at baseline and at least annually (BNF). Warfarin is retained for specific situations, with choice governed by indication, renal function, pregnancy and the need for reversibility.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the mechanism and route of heparins (UFH/LMWH)?
options: Vitamin K antagonist; oral
Direct factor Xa inhibition; oral
Activate antithrombin → inactivate thrombin + factor Xa; parenteral (SC/IV)
Direct thrombin inhibition; oral
Inhibit VKORC1; parenteral
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Activate antithrombin → inactivate thrombin + factor Xa; parenteral (SC/IV)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Heparins activate antithrombin to inactivate thrombin and factor Xa, and are given parenterally (SC/IV).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient with severe renal impairment needs heparin anticoagulation. Why is LMWH avoided, and what is used instead?
options: LMWH is hepatically cleared, so it accumulates in liver disease rather than renal failure — use warfarin
LMWH requires APTT monitoring; use a DOAC
LMWH crosses the placenta; use aspirin
LMWH has no renal handling issues at all, so no dose change is needed at any level of renal function
LMWH is renally cleared, so it is avoided/reduced in severe renal impairment — use UFH instead
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: LMWH is renally cleared, so it is avoided/reduced in severe renal impairment — use UFH instead
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: LMWH is renally cleared, so below a CrCl of 30 mL/min the treatment dose is reduced to enoxaparin 1 mg/kg once daily (the twice-daily regimen is dropped) and prophylaxis to 20 mg once daily; below 15 mL/min UFH is used instead.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which heparin is monitored by APTT and chosen when rapid on/off control is needed?
options: LMWH
UFH (unfractionated heparin)
Dabigatran
Warfarin
Apixaban
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: UFH (unfractionated heparin)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: UFH has a short half-life, is monitored by APTT titrated to a ratio of 1.5–2.5 times control (whereas LMWH needs none), and is used when rapid on/off is needed (peri-procedure, high bleeding risk) and in severe renal impairment.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on heparin develops a falling platelet count ~7 days in and a new thrombosis. What is the diagnosis and the immediate action?
options: Simple bleeding from heparin with consumption of platelets; give more heparin to maintain anticoagulation
Osteoporosis; continue heparin
Hyperkalaemia; give insulin only
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — an immune-mediated, paradoxically prothrombotic platelet drop; stop heparin and switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant
Warfarin-induced skin necrosis from protein C depletion; start warfarin to correct the imbalance
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — an immune-mediated, paradoxically prothrombotic platelet drop; stop heparin and switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: HIT is an immune-mediated platelet drop ~5-10 days in that is paradoxically prothrombotic; the action is to stop heparin and switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the reversal agent for heparin?
options: Protamine sulphate
Vitamin K
Idarucizumab
Andexanet alfa
Prothrombin complex concentrate
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Protamine sulphate
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Heparin is reversed with protamine sulphate — reversal is complete for unfractionated heparin but only partial for LMWH.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the mechanism of warfarin?
options: Activates antithrombin, which then inactivates thrombin and factor Xa in the circulation
Directly inhibits factor Xa
Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) → reduces vitamin-K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X (and proteins C & S)
Directly inhibits thrombin
Binds irreversibly to platelet receptors to prevent aggregation and thrombus formation
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) → reduces vitamin-K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X (and proteins C & S)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), reducing vitamin-K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C & S).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the INR target for most warfarin indications, and for mechanical valves?
options: 1-2 for most; 2-3 for valves
3-4 for most; 4-5 for valves
2.5-3.5 for most; 2-3 for valves
No target is needed
2-3 for most; 2.5-3.5 for mechanical valves
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: 2-3 for most; 2.5-3.5 for mechanical valves
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Warfarin is monitored by INR with a target of 2-3 for most indications and 2.5-3.5 for mechanical valves — a narrow therapeutic window.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Why is LMWH bridging used when warfarin is started for acute VTE, and what rare complication relates to this?
options: Because warfarin works instantly, so the only risk at initiation is bleeding rather than clotting
Because warfarin takes days to work and proteins C & S drop first, causing transient hypercoagulability; skin necrosis is the rare consequence
Because warfarin is renally cleared and accumulates at initiation; the complication is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
Because LMWH raises the INR; the complication is osteoporosis
Because warfarin needs APTT monitoring; the complication is hyperkalaemia
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Because warfarin takes days to work and proteins C & S drop first, causing transient hypercoagulability; skin necrosis is the rare consequence
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Warfarin takes several days to become effective, and the anticoagulant proteins C & S drop first, causing transient hypercoagulability — so LMWH bridging covers acute VTE for at least 5 days AND until the INR has been 2 or above for 24 hours, whichever is longer. Bridging is not routine when warfarin is started for AF, and warfarin-induced skin necrosis is the rare consequence.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on warfarin starts a new drug and the INR rises, increasing bleeding risk. Which drug is a P450 inhibitor responsible for this?
options: Rifampicin
Carbamazepine
Phenytoin
Amiodarone
St John's wort
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Amiodarone
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: P450 inhibitors raise the warfarin effect and INR (bleeding risk) — these include ciprofloxacin, macrolides, acute alcohol, amiodarone, allopurinol, isoniazid, omeprazole, SSRIs and cranberry/grapefruit juice. Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin and St John's wort are inducers that lower the INR.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following is a P450 inducer that reduces the warfarin effect and lowers the INR?
options: Rifampicin
Erythromycin
Ciprofloxacin
Allopurinol
Omeprazole
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Rifampicin
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: P450 inducers reduce the warfarin effect and lower the INR — these include carbamazepine, rifampicin, chronic alcohol, phenytoin and St John's wort.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A warfarinised patient presents with significant bleeding. What is the appropriate reversal?
options: Withhold warfarin only
Oral vitamin K alone
IV vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC, e.g. Beriplex)
Protamine sulphate
Idarucizumab
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: IV vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC, e.g. Beriplex)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Significant bleeding on warfarin is reversed with vitamin K 5 mg by slow IV injection plus prothrombin complex concentrate 25–50 units/kg, without waiting for the INR; FFP 15 mL/kg is second-line if PCC is unavailable. With a high INR and no bleeding, the action depends on the band: INR 5–8 — withhold 1–2 doses, no vitamin K; INR above 8 — vitamin K 1–5 mg orally.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient with a mechanical heart valve needs long-term anticoagulation. Which agent is appropriate and why?
options: A DOAC, because it needs no monitoring
LMWH indefinitely, because it is oral
Aspirin, because it prevents valve thrombosis
Dabigatran, because it is licensed for mechanical valves
Warfarin, because DOACs are contraindicated in mechanical heart valves
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Warfarin, because DOACs are contraindicated in mechanical heart valves
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Warfarin is still preferred over DOACs for mechanical heart valves, antiphospholipid syndrome, severe renal impairment and moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis — the 'DOAC contraindicated' list.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A pregnant woman requires anticoagulation. Which agent is appropriate, and why are the others avoided?
options: Warfarin, because it doesn't cross the placenta
LMWH, because warfarin is teratogenic (warfarin embryopathy) and DOACs are unsafe
A DOAC, because it needs no monitoring
Aspirin, because it is an anticoagulant
UFH only, because LMWH is contraindicated in pregnancy
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: LMWH, because warfarin is teratogenic (warfarin embryopathy) and DOACs are unsafe
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: In pregnancy, LMWH is used because it is safe and doesn't cross the placenta, whereas warfarin is contraindicated (teratogenic — warfarin embryopathy) and DOACs are unsafe.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which DOAC class do apixaban, rivaroxaban and edoxaban belong to, and what reverses them?
options: Direct thrombin inhibitors; reversed by idarucizumab
Vitamin K antagonists; reversed by vitamin K
Heparins; reversed by protamine
Factor Xa inhibitors ('-xabans'); andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban (PCC for edoxaban)
Antiplatelets; no reversal agent
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Factor Xa inhibitors ('-xabans'); andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban (PCC for edoxaban)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Apixaban, rivaroxaban and edoxaban are factor Xa inhibitors ('-xabans'); andexanet alfa is licensed to reverse apixaban and rivaroxaban only, and PCC is used for edoxaban. Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor reversed by idarucizumab.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran?
options: Idarucizumab
Andexanet alfa
Protamine sulphate
Vitamin K
Fresh frozen plasma
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Idarucizumab
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, is reversed with idarucizumab.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following is a recognised caution/contraindication for DOACs?
options: They are first-line for mechanical heart valves, having replaced warfarin in that indication
They are preferred in severe renal impairment
They are contraindicated in pregnancy/breastfeeding and not used for mechanical valves or antiphospholipid syndrome
They require routine INR monitoring
They are safe at any level of renal function and need no dose adjustment whatever the CrCl
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: They are contraindicated in pregnancy/breastfeeding and not used for mechanical valves or antiphospholipid syndrome
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: DOACs are contraindicated in pregnancy/breastfeeding (use LMWH) and are not used for mechanical valves or antiphospholipid syndrome. They also need dose attention in renal impairment — apixaban is avoided if CrCl is below 15 mL/min with dose reduction at 15–29, and rivaroxaban is avoided below 15 (BNF) — and dabigatran increases dyspepsia and GI bleeding.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: For inpatient VTE prophylaxis, which agent is preferred?
options: Warfarin
Dabigatran
Aspirin
UFH by default
LMWH
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: LMWH
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: LMWH is the preferred agent for inpatient VTE prophylaxis — enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily, or dalteparin 5000 units subcutaneously once daily, as a fixed dose.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: In atrial fibrillation, which two scores are balanced when deciding on anticoagulation, and what does each represent?
options: CURB-65 (bleeding risk) vs Wells (clot risk), as used in atrial fibrillation
ORBIT, or the older HAS-BLED (bleeding) vs CHA₂DS₂-VASc (stroke risk)
GRACE (bleeding risk) vs TIMI (clot risk), as used in atrial fibrillation
HAS-BLED (stroke risk) vs CHA₂DS₂-VASc (bleeding risk) — the two reversed
Child-Pugh (bleeding risk) vs MELD (clot risk), as used in atrial fibrillation
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: ORBIT, or the older HAS-BLED (bleeding) vs CHA₂DS₂-VASc (stroke risk)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The major complication of anticoagulation is bleeding (GI, intracranial). In AF, bleeding risk is balanced against CHA₂DS₂-VASc (thrombotic/stroke risk); NICE now specifies ORBIT for bleeding-risk assessment, and a high bleeding score should prompt modification of reversible risk factors rather than withholding anticoagulation.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which DOAC has the most favourable bleeding profile, especially gastrointestinal?
options: Rivaroxaban
Dabigatran
Edoxaban
Apixaban
Warfarin
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Apixaban
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Apixaban has the most favourable bleeding profile, especially gastrointestinal.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which statement about palliative care is correct according to the WHO definition?
options: It is care provided only in the last days of life, once all active treatment has been withdrawn
It is holistic physical care that deliberately excludes the psychological and spiritual dimensions
It is quality-of-life care that can only be delivered in a hospice rather than at home or in hospital
It is holistic care focused on quality of life in life-limiting illness and can run alongside active treatment
It is care that replaces all active treatment as soon as an illness is judged to be life-limiting
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: It is holistic care focused on quality of life in life-limiting illness and can run alongside active treatment
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Palliative care (WHO) is holistic care focused on quality of life in life-limiting illness — physical, psychological, social and spiritual — and is not just end-of-life; it can run alongside active treatment.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What are the four core anticipatory ('just in case') medications prescribed in advance for a dying patient?
options: Opioid, antiemetic, antisecretory, and sedative
Antibiotic, antiemetic, diuretic, laxative
Steroid, antiemetic, antihypertensive, and anticoagulant
Opioid, antibiotic, antisecretory, and diuretic
Antiemetic, laxative, PPI, and sedative
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Opioid, antiemetic, antisecretory, and sedative
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The four core anticipatory medications are an opioid (pain/breathlessness, e.g. morphine), an antiemetic (e.g. haloperidol/levomepromazine/cyclizine), an antisecretory (hyoscine or glycopyrronium for the 'death rattle'), and a sedative (midazolam for agitation/terminal restlessness) — prescribed as PRN subcutaneous injections. A syringe driver is not prescribed in anticipation; it is started only when symptoms recur.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A palliative patient is on regular morphine totalling 60mg/day. What is the correct breakthrough dose?
options: 60mg (the full daily dose)
30mg (half the daily dose)
10mg (the total daily dose divided by 6)
6mg (a fixed dose)
20mg (a third of the daily dose)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: 10mg (the total daily dose divided by 6)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The breakthrough dose = total daily opioid dose ÷ 6. For 60mg/day, that is 60÷6 = 10mg PRN. If ≥3 breakthrough doses are used in 24h, the regular dose is increased by the same amount.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient is on 60mg/day of oral morphine and needs to be converted to subcutaneous morphine via a syringe driver. What is the correct SC dose?
options: 60mg (no change)
20mg (divide by 3)
6mg (divide by 10)
120mg (multiply by 2)
30mg (divide the total daily oral dose by 2)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: 30mg (divide the total daily oral dose by 2)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Oral → subcutaneous morphine: divide the total 24-hour dose by 2. So 60mg oral → 30mg SC per 24h. 20mg would be correct if converting to SC diamorphine (divide by 3), not morphine — ratios are drug-specific and must never be carried across. (Codeine → oral morphine: divide by 10.)

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Why is diamorphine preferred over morphine for syringe drivers in palliative care?
options: It is less potent than morphine, so a larger volume can safely be given through the driver
It is highly water-soluble, so it can be given in small volumes and mixed with other drugs
It has no active metabolites, so it can be mixed with other drugs without risk of precipitation
It bypasses first-pass metabolism, so a smaller volume achieves the same systemic effect
It is cheaper than morphine, which matters when a driver runs continuously over 24 hours
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: It is highly water-soluble, so it can be given in small volumes and mixed with other drugs
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Diamorphine is highly water-soluble, making it preferred for syringe drivers (it can be given in small volumes and mixed with other drugs). Oral morphine is converted to SC diamorphine by dividing by 3.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A palliative patient with renal impairment is on morphine and develops confusion, myoclonus and pinpoint pupils. What are the appropriate steps?
options: Increase the morphine dose, ensure hydration, and give naloxone only if respiratory depression is life-threatening
Continue the current dose but give routine naloxone for all opioid toxicity, whether or not breathing is compromised
Add a second strong opioid alongside the morphine, ensure hydration, and withhold naloxone under all circumstances
Reduce the dose or rotate the opioid (switch to oxycodone), ensure hydration, and give naloxone only if respiratory depression is life-threatening
Stop all analgesia abruptly, restrict fluids, and give naloxone only if respiratory depression is life-threatening
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Reduce the dose or rotate the opioid (switch to oxycodone), ensure hydration, and give naloxone only if respiratory depression is life-threatening
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Opioid toxicity (drowsiness, confusion, myoclonus, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression) is managed by reducing the dose/rotating the opioid and ensuring hydration. In mild-moderate renal impairment morphine accumulates (active metabolites), so switch to oxycodone; in severe renal impairment (eGFR under 30) oxycodone also accumulates and alfentanil or fentanyl is preferred. Naloxone is used only if respiratory depression is life-threatening (small titrated doses to avoid precipitating severe pain/withdrawal).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which laxative approach is correct when starting a palliative patient on opioids?
options: Always co-prescribe a laxative — a stimulant (senna) ± softener/osmotic — and avoid bulk-forming laxatives in the dying patient
No laxative is needed, as opioid-related constipation is uncommon and usually resolves without treatment
Use only bulk-forming laxatives, which are the agents of choice for the dying patient on strong opioids
Give a laxative only once constipation has actually developed, rather than co-prescribing it from the outset
Use an antisecretory drug such as hyoscine instead, since it addresses the same underlying bowel problem
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Always co-prescribe a laxative — a stimulant (senna) ± softener/osmotic — and avoid bulk-forming laxatives in the dying patient
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Constipation is near-universal with opioids, so always co-prescribe a laxative — stimulant (senna) ± softener/osmotic (macrogol/docusate). Bulk-forming laxatives should be avoided in the dying patient.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A dying patient develops audible upper-airway secretions ('death rattle'). Which drug is first-line, and by what route?
options: Midazolam (a benzodiazepine sedative), given orally
Cyclizine (an H1 receptor antagonist), given IV
Hyoscine hydrobromide (a muscarinic antagonist), given SC
Ondansetron (a 5-HT3 antagonist), given orally
Dexamethasone (a corticosteroid), given IM
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Hyoscine hydrobromide (a muscarinic antagonist), given SC
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Hyoscine hydrobromide, a muscarinic antagonist, is used for respiratory secretions ('death rattle'), given SC. Hyoscine butylbromide and glycopyrronium are equally effective and, unlike hydrobromide, do not cross the blood-brain barrier — hydrobromide can cause sedation, confusion or paradoxical agitation. Bowel colic is treated with hyoscine butylbromide.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A palliative patient with raised intracranial pressure due to brain metastases has vomiting. Which antiemetic is first-line for intracranial causes?
options: Metoclopramide (a D2 antagonist with prokinetic action)
Ondansetron (a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist)
Haloperidol (a D2 antagonist acting at the chemoreceptor trigger zone)
Hyoscine (a muscarinic antagonist with antisecretory action)
Cyclizine (an H1 receptor antagonist acting on the vomiting centre)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Cyclizine (an H1 receptor antagonist acting on the vomiting centre)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Cyclizine (an H1 receptor antagonist acting on the vomiting centre) is first-line for intracranial causes of nausea. Metoclopramide (D2 antagonist/prokinetic) is used for GI dysmotility, haloperidol for chemical/metabolic and opioid-induced nausea, and ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist) is reserved for chemotherapy- or radiotherapy-induced nausea, as it worsens opioid constipation.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A palliative patient with gastric stasis has nausea. Which antiemetic is most appropriate, and why?
options: Cyclizine, because it acts on the vomiting centre
Metoclopramide, a D2 antagonist with prokinetic action
Hyoscine, an antisecretory
Dexamethasone, a steroid
Midazolam, a sedative
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Metoclopramide, a D2 antagonist with prokinetic action
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Metoclopramide (a D2 antagonist with prokinetic action) is used for GI dysmotility/gastric stasis — but avoid it in complete bowel obstruction or colic, where prokinesis worsens pain. Cyclizine does act on the vomiting centre, but its antimuscarinic action opposes metoclopramide's prokinetic effect, so it is the wrong choice in gastric stasis. Ondansetron is for chemotherapy-induced nausea.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A palliative patient has agitation and terminal restlessness. What is the first-line drug and route, and what must be excluded?
options: Cyclizine orally, converting to a syringe driver if needed; exclude infection as the underlying trigger
Dexamethasone IM, converting to a syringe driver if needed; exclude raised intracranial pressure as the cause
Hyoscine SC, converting to a syringe driver if needed; exclude retained respiratory secretions as the cause
Midazolam SC PRN, converting to a syringe driver if repeated doses are needed; exclude reversible causes such as urinary retention, pain and constipation
Ondansetron IV, converting to a syringe driver if needed; exclude nausea as the underlying trigger
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Midazolam SC PRN, converting to a syringe driver if repeated doses are needed; exclude reversible causes such as urinary retention, pain and constipation
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Midazolam SC PRN is first-line for agitation/terminal restlessness, converted to a syringe driver only if repeated doses are needed (haloperidol or levomepromazine are alternatives). Reversible causes such as urinary retention, pain and constipation should be excluded.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How is malignant bone pain from metastases best managed?
options: Analgesics (WHO ladder) plus bisphosphonates (zoledronate) and radiotherapy (single fraction for bone mets)
Antisecretory drugs alone, such as hyoscine or glycopyrronium given via a syringe driver
Midazolam alone, titrated upwards until the pain from the bone metastases settles
Cyclizine and dexamethasone, with no role for radiotherapy or bone-modifying agents
Hyoscine and a laxative, with analgesia withheld because of the risk of opioid toxicity
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Analgesics (WHO ladder) plus bisphosphonates (zoledronate) and radiotherapy (single fraction for bone mets)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Metastatic bone pain is managed with WHO-ladder analgesics plus bisphosphonates (zoledronate reduces skeletal events) and radiotherapy (single fraction for bone mets). A pathological fracture is managed with orthopaedic surgery then radiotherapy.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which route of administration has 100% bioavailability, the fastest onset, and is unaffected by first-pass metabolism, but carries a risk of phlebitis and air embolism?
options: Oral
Sublingual
Intravenous (IV)
Rectal
Transdermal
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Intravenous (IV)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The IV route has 100% bioavailability, the fastest onset (5–10 min), and is not affected by first-pass metabolism, but carries risks of infection, phlebitis and air embolism.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which route is contraindicated in haemophilia due to the risk of a massive haematoma?
options: Subcutaneous
Sublingual
Inhaled
Rectal
Intramuscular (IM)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Intramuscular (IM)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The intramuscular route is contraindicated in haemophilia because of the risk of a massive haematoma. It has high but variable bioavailability (only IV is 100% by definition) with a max volume of 5ml (e.g. adrenaline, glucagon, vaccines).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Why does sublingual GTN act rapidly and avoid the large reduction in drug availability seen with some oral drugs?
options: It is highly water-soluble, so a large dose can be dissolved in the small volume the route allows
It bypasses first-pass (hepatic) metabolism, which can otherwise reduce oral drug availability by up to 90%
It is given at a very high dose by this route, which overwhelms the liver's capacity to metabolise it
It is absorbed directly across the gastric mucosa, which drains into the systemic rather than portal circulation
It has a long half-life, so enough drug survives hepatic metabolism to give a reliable clinical effect
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: It bypasses first-pass (hepatic) metabolism, which can otherwise reduce oral drug availability by up to 90%
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The sublingual route bypasses first-pass metabolism, giving fast absorption (e.g. GTN, buprenorphine, midazolam). The oral route has variable bioavailability because hepatic first-pass can reduce availability by up to 90% for some drugs.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient in status epilepticus in the community cannot have IV access. Which route/agent is appropriate?
options: Inhaled salbutamol
Topical GTN
Buccal midazolam
Rectal (PR) diazepam
Intrathecal chemotherapy
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Buccal midazolam
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: (NICE) recommends buccal midazolam first-line for prolonged or repeated convulsive seizures in the community, with rectal diazepam as the alternative if buccal midazolam is unavailable or preferred. Both work because they avoid the oral route in a patient who cannot swallow.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: According to NICE maintenance fluid requirements, what is the daily water requirement?
options: 25–30 mL/kg/day
10–15 mL/kg/day
50–60 mL/kg/day
1 mL/kg/day
100 mL/kg/day
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: 25–30 mL/kg/day
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: NICE maintenance fluid requirements are: water 25–30 mL/kg/day, electrolytes 1 mmol/kg/day of Na, K and Cl, and glucose 50–100 g/day.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A hypovolaemic patient needs a fluid challenge. What is the standard approach, and how is it modified in the elderly or those with heart failure/CKD?
options: 500ml crystalloid over 4 hours with no modification for the elderly or those with heart failure or CKD, repeated indefinitely
2000ml crystalloid as an immediate bolus for everyone regardless of age or comorbidity, without senior review
500ml crystalloid STAT over 15 minutes, reduced to 250ml in the elderly/HF/CKD, repeated up to 2000ml then senior review
Colloid only, given as 500ml STAT over 15 minutes and repeated up to 2000ml before seeking senior review
Oral rehydration only, reduced in the elderly or those with heart failure or CKD, with senior review at 2000ml
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: 500ml crystalloid STAT over 15 minutes, reduced to 250ml in the elderly/HF/CKD, repeated up to 2000ml then senior review
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: A fluid challenge is 500ml crystalloid STAT (15 mins), reduced to 250ml in the elderly/HF/CKD, repeated up to 2000ml before seeking senior review.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which crystalloid is preferred to avoid hyperchloraemic acidosis?
options: 0.9% normal saline
5% dextrose
Albumin
10% dextrose
Hartmann's (a balanced crystalloid)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Hartmann's (a balanced crystalloid)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Hartmann's is a balanced crystalloid preferred to avoid hyperchloraemic acidosis. Colloids (albumin) remain intravascular longer but carry a risk of anaphylaxis and are rarely used.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the maximum safe rate for IV potassium administration, and why?
options: 40 mmol/hour; risk of hypokalaemia
20 mmol/hour; faster rates risk a fatal cardiac arrhythmia
100 mmol/hour; no risk
As a rapid bolus for speed
There is no maximum rate
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: 20 mmol/hour; faster rates risk a fatal cardiac arrhythmia
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Potassium should never be given faster than 20 mmol/hour because of the risk of a fatal cardiac arrhythmia, and never as a bolus. Peripheral lines allow a max 40 mmol/L concentration; central lines can give more concentrated K⁺ with continuous cardiac monitoring.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient describes burning, shooting pain with tingling and allodynia. What type of pain is this, and why do opioids work poorly?
options: Nociceptive pain; opioids are highly effective
Acute pain; treat with the WHO ladder alone
Chronic primary pain with no identifiable cause; treat with regular NSAIDs and a proton pump inhibitor
Neuropathic pain (nerve damage/dysfunction); opioids work poorly, so specific neuropathic agents are used
Referred pain from a visceral structure; treat with regular paracetamol and reassurance
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Neuropathic pain (nerve damage/dysfunction); opioids work poorly, so specific neuropathic agents are used
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Burning, shooting, tingling pain with allodynia is neuropathic (nerve damage/dysfunction). Opioids work poorly on neuropathic pain, so specific neuropathic agents are used instead.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How is chronic pain defined by duration?
options: Pain lasting more than 3 months
Pain lasting more than 1 week
Pain lasting more than 6 weeks
Pain lasting more than 1 year
Any pain requiring opioids
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Pain lasting more than 3 months
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Chronic pain is defined as pain lasting more than 3 months.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which tool is used to identify whether pain has a neuropathic component?
options: The Visual Analogue Scale
The Glasgow Coma Scale
The DN4 questionnaire (≥4/10 suggests neuropathic pain)
SOCRATES only
The Numerical Rating Scale
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: The DN4 questionnaire (≥4/10 suggests neuropathic pain)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The DN4 questionnaire identifies neuropathic pain (a score ≥4/10 suggests neuropathic). VAS and NRS measure intensity, and SOCRATES characterises pain.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: According to the WHO analgesic ladder, which drugs are used at Step 2 (moderate pain)?
options: Paracetamol ± NSAID
Strong opioids — morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl
Nerve blocks and spinal analgesia
Antidepressants and anticonvulsants
Weak opioids — codeine, dihydrocodeine, tramadol (+ non-opioid ± adjuvant)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Weak opioids — codeine, dihydrocodeine, tramadol (+ non-opioid ± adjuvant)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Step 2 (moderate pain) uses weak opioids — codeine 30–60 mg 4-hourly PRN (max 240 mg/24 h), dihydrocodeine 30 mg 4–6-hourly PRN (max 180 mg/24 h), or tramadol 50–100 mg 4–6-hourly PRN (max 400 mg/24 h) — with a non-opioid ± adjuvant. Step 1 is non-opioid (paracetamol 1 g QDS, max 4 g/24 h, ± NSAID) and Step 3 is strong opioids.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient presents with severe pain. According to WHO ladder principles, what is appropriate?
options: Always start at Step 1 and progress slowly
Leapfrogging is allowed — start directly at Step 3, with a fast-acting rescue dose for breakthrough pain
Use only PRN dosing, since regular dosing causes tolerance and dependence to develop faster
Avoid opioids entirely and manage severe cancer pain with non-opioid adjuvants alone
Start at Step 2 and remain there
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Leapfrogging is allowed — start directly at Step 3, with a fast-acting rescue dose for breakthrough pain
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The ladder principles ('by the mouth, by the clock, by the ladder, for the individual') allow leapfrogging — severe pain can start directly at Step 3, with a fast-acting rescue dose for breakthrough pain: immediate-release morphine, one sixth of the total 24-hour oral morphine dose (5 mg if the total is 30 mg/24 h). Regular (not just PRN) dosing is used for continuous pain.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which cautions apply to NSAID use?
options: They are safe in all patients provided the course is limited to fewer than fourteen days
They cause hepatotoxicity only, so the sole precaution needed is monitoring liver function
They must always be co-prescribed with a laxative
GI ulcer/bleed, renal impairment, cardiovascular disease and asthma; avoid in CKD/PUD/heart failure and co-prescribe a PPI
They lower the seizure threshold
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: GI ulcer/bleed, renal impairment, cardiovascular disease and asthma; avoid in CKD/PUD/heart failure and co-prescribe a PPI
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit COX → reduced prostaglandins, with cautions of GI ulcer/bleed, renal impairment, cardiovascular disease and asthma. Avoid in CKD/PUD/heart failure, co-prescribe a PPI (omeprazole 20 mg OD) for as long as the NSAID continues, and use the lowest effective dose for the shortest period — ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food, or naproxen 250–500 mg BD with food.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Codeine is a prodrug. Why does its effect vary between individuals?
options: It is metabolised to morphine by CYP2D6, so poor metabolisers get no analgesia and ultra-rapid metabolisers get toxic levels
It is inactivated by the liver at the same rate in everyone, so the response is predictable
It works directly without metabolism
It is excreted renally unchanged, so its effect depends only on renal function
It is a strong opioid at Step 3
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: It is metabolised to morphine by CYP2D6, so poor metabolisers get no analgesia and ultra-rapid metabolisers get toxic levels
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Codeine is a µ-opioid prodrug converted to morphine by CYP2D6. Poor metabolisers get no analgesia, while ultra-rapid metabolisers get dangerous morphine levels. (Tramadol additionally lowers the seizure threshold and is serotonergic.)

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What should ALWAYS be co-prescribed when starting an opioid, and why?
options: A PPI, to prevent GI bleeding
Naloxone, taken regularly
A laxative (stimulant ± softener), because constipation is near-universal
An NSAID, for synergy
An antidepressant
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: A laxative (stimulant ± softener), because constipation is near-universal
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: A laxative should always be co-prescribed with opioids because constipation is near-universal — senna 15 mg at night, ± docusate 100 mg BD if stools are hard. A PRN antiemetic is also considered when starting: metoclopramide 10 mg up to TDS (max 5 days — MHRA) or cyclizine 50 mg up to TDS.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on opioids becomes drowsy and confused with pinpoint pupils and myoclonus, but is rousable with a respiratory rate of 14. What is the management approach?
options: Increase the opioid dose
Give naloxone routinely for any sign of toxicity, titrated to the level of consciousness
Add a second strong opioid to provide background analgesia while the first is reduced
Give an NSAID
Reduce the dose or rotate the opioid; give naloxone only if respiratory depression is life-threatening (RR under 8)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Reduce the dose or rotate the opioid; give naloxone only if respiratory depression is life-threatening (RR under 8)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Opioid toxicity (drowsiness → confusion, pinpoint pupils, myoclonus) in a rousable patient with an adequate respiratory rate is managed by reducing the dose or rotating the opioid. Naloxone is reserved for life-threatening respiratory depression — 400 micrograms IV, repeated every 2–3 minutes to a maximum of 10 mg; in a patient taking opioids for pain, dilute 400 micrograms to 10 mL and give 100-microgram boluses, titrating to respiratory rate rather than conscious level.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient with significant renal impairment needs a strong opioid. Why is morphine problematic, and what is preferred?
options: Morphine is fine; use it at standard dose
Morphine accumulates due to active metabolites, so use oxycodone, or fentanyl/buprenorphine
Morphine is too weak; use fentanyl at high dose
Use codeine instead
Avoid all opioids
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Morphine accumulates due to active metabolites, so use oxycodone, or fentanyl/buprenorphine
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: In renal impairment, morphine accumulates due to active metabolites, so oxycodone (or fentanyl/buprenorphine) is preferred.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which statement about patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) is correct?
options: An oral opioid taken PRN by the patient whenever the pain becomes troublesome
A device that requires no monitoring once the initial programming has been set
Other PRN opioids should always be co-prescribed
An IV strong opioid, patient-triggered and locked out to prevent overdose; avoid other PRN opioids alongside
It is used for stable chronic pain only
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: An IV strong opioid, patient-triggered and locked out to prevent overdose; avoid other PRN opioids alongside
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: PCA is an IV strong opioid, patient-triggered and locked to prevent overdose. It needs anaesthetic input with naloxone/antiemetic/atropine available, and other PRN opioids should be avoided alongside.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Opioid patches (buprenorphine, fentanyl) are appropriate for which situation?
options: Stable chronic pain as background analgesia, not acute titration
Rapid titration of acute severe pain
Breakthrough pain only
First-line for neuropathic pain
Post-operative day one
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Stable chronic pain as background analgesia, not acute titration
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Opioid patches (buprenorphine, fentanyl) are for stable chronic pain as background analgesia — not for acute titration.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: According to NICE, what are the first-line options for neuropathic pain?
options: Morphine or oxycodone, titrated against the pain in the same way as for nociceptive pain
Paracetamol and NSAIDs
One of four: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, or pregabalin (switch if one fails)
Codeine and tramadol, escalating through the WHO ladder as the pain worsens
Corticosteroids
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: One of four: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, or pregabalin (switch if one fails)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: NICE recommends one of four first-line agents for neuropathic pain — amitriptyline 10 mg at night titrated to 25–75 mg, duloxetine 60 mg OD, gabapentin 300 mg OD increasing over 3 days to TDS then to a maximum of 3.6 g/24 h, or pregabalin 75 mg BD to a maximum of 600 mg/24 h — switching if one fails. Opioids work poorly.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which agent is specifically used for trigeminal neuralgia?
options: Morphine
Paracetamol
Ibuprofen
Oxycodone
Carbamazepine
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Carbamazepine
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Carbamazepine is used specifically for trigeminal neuralgia — 100 mg once or twice daily, increased in 100–200 mg steps until the pain is controlled. Tramadol may be used as rescue only, and capsaicin cream for localised neuropathic pain.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient has chronic primary pain (e.g. fibromyalgia) with no underlying cause. What does NICE recommend? (high-yield)
options: Long-term strong opioids, titrated to effect, with a laxative co-prescribed from the outset
Avoid most analgesia (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids/gabapentinoids); offer exercise, psychological therapy, and consider an antidepressant
High-dose NSAIDs with a PPI, continued long term with renal function monitoring
Gabapentin as first-line
Regular codeine
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Avoid most analgesia (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids/gabapentinoids); offer exercise, psychological therapy, and consider an antidepressant
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: For chronic primary pain (no underlying cause, e.g. fibromyalgia), NICE recommends avoiding most analgesia (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids/gabapentinoids) and instead using exercise, psychological therapy (CBT/ACT), and considering an antidepressant such as duloxetine or amitriptyline — a high-yield SBA point.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which adjuvant is most appropriate for metastatic bone pain?
options: Gabapentin
Amitriptyline
A benzodiazepine
Bisphosphonates
Capsaicin cream
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Bisphosphonates
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Bisphosphonates are the adjuvant for metastatic bone pain. Antidepressants/anticonvulsants are for neuropathic pain, corticosteroids for inflammatory/nerve compression/raised ICP, and benzodiazepines for muscle spasm.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How is post-operative pain typically managed?
options: Regular paracetamol + NSAID + PRN immediate-release opioid (not modified-release), wound infiltration and PCA, stepping down daily
A single dose of paracetamol on return from theatre, with further analgesia only if requested
Neuropathic agents only
Opioid patches, which allow rapid titration against a falling post-operative requirement
Avoiding all analgesia
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Regular paracetamol + NSAID + PRN immediate-release opioid (not modified-release), wound infiltration and PCA, stepping down daily
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Post-operative pain is managed with regular paracetamol 1 g QDS and an NSAID plus a PRN IMMEDIATE-RELEASE opioid, local anaesthetic wound infiltration and PCA, stepped down daily. Modified-release opioids are not used for acute post-operative pain — they cannot be titrated against a rapidly falling requirement and they accumulate in the opioid-naive.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: During which period is the fetus most vulnerable to structural malformations from teratogenic drugs?
options: The 3rd trimester
The immediate postnatal period
Only at term
The 1st trimester (organogenesis)
The 2nd trimester only
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: The 1st trimester (organogenesis)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The 1st trimester (organogenesis) is most vulnerable to structural malformations. Some drugs (ACEi, NSAIDs) instead harm specifically in the 2nd/3rd trimester, causing growth/functional/organ damage.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A pregnant woman with a previous DVT needs anticoagulation. Warfarin is teratogenic in pregnancy. What is the safe alternative and why?
options: LMWH, because it does not cross the placenta
A DOAC, because it is renally cleared
Aspirin, because it is a mild agent
Continue warfarin at a lower dose
Stop all anticoagulation
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: LMWH, because it does not cross the placenta
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Warfarin causes warfarin embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses, limb hypoplasia) from weeks 6–12, with CNS damage and haemorrhage from later exposure. LMWH is the safe alternative because it does not cross the placenta. DOACs are also avoided. Mechanical heart valves are the exception — anticoagulation there is a specialist decision, and warfarin may be continued because LMWH carries a higher risk of valve thrombosis.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A woman in her second trimester on an ACE inhibitor for hypertension is found to have oligohydramnios. What fetal effects are associated with ACEi/ARBs, and what should she be switched to?
options: Neural tube defects and spina bifida; switch to sodium valproate, lamotrigine or levetiracetam
Ebstein's anomaly of the tricuspid valve; switch to lithium under specialist supervision
Oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure/anuria, skull and lung hypoplasia; switch to labetalol, nifedipine, or methyldopa
Tooth discolouration and impaired bone growth; switch to a tetracycline such as doxycycline
Phocomelia and limb reduction defects; switch to thalidomide or leflunomide instead
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure/anuria, skull and lung hypoplasia; switch to labetalol, nifedipine, or methyldopa
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: In the 2nd/3rd trimester, ACEi/ARBs cause oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure/anuria, and skull and lung hypoplasia. Safe alternatives are labetalol, nifedipine, and methyldopa.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which antiepileptic drug is considered the highest-risk in pregnancy, and what characteristic defect does it cause?
options: Lamotrigine; cardiac defects including Ebstein's anomaly, with developmental delay
Levetiracetam; cleft palate and fetal hydantoin syndrome with developmental delay
Phenytoin; sensorineural deafness and neural tube defects with developmental delay
Carbamazepine; phocomelia and limb reduction defects with developmental delay
Sodium valproate; neural tube defects (spina bifida) and fetal valproate syndrome with developmental delay
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Sodium valproate; neural tube defects (spina bifida) and fetal valproate syndrome with developmental delay
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Sodium valproate is the highest-risk AED, causing neural tube defects (spina bifida), fetal valproate syndrome and developmental delay. It must not be used in any woman or girl able to have children unless the conditions of the Pregnancy Prevention Programme are met, and must not be started in any new patient under 55, male or female, unless two specialists independently document that there is no alternative (MHRA). Preferred alternatives are lamotrigine and levetiracetam.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A woman with epilepsy is planning pregnancy. Which regimen is most appropriate?
options: Continue valproate at the lowest dose
Switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam with folate supplementation
Switch to phenytoin
Stop all antiepileptics
Add carbamazepine to valproate
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam with folate supplementation
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: For epilepsy in pregnancy, avoid valproate and phenytoin and use lamotrigine or levetiracetam with folate. Teratogenic AEDs should ideally be switched pre-conception.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A pregnant woman is inadvertently exposed to lithium in the first trimester. Which characteristic cardiac defect is associated with lithium?
options: Tetralogy of Fallot
Ventricular septal defect
Patent ductus arteriosus
Ebstein's anomaly (a tricuspid valve defect)
Coarctation of the aorta
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Ebstein's anomaly (a tricuspid valve defect)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Lithium is associated with Ebstein's anomaly (a tricuspid valve cardiac defect). It requires careful specialist review in pregnancy.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A woman on methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis wishes to conceive. What advice is correct?
options: Methotrexate is an abortifacient causing multiple malformations and must be stopped before conception — at least 3 months, or 1 month in women per UK guidance
Methotrexate may be continued throughout pregnancy provided the dose is kept low and folate is co-prescribed
Methotrexate need only be stopped in the third trimester, as the fetal risk is confined to late gestation
Methotrexate should be switched to isotretinoin before conception, as retinoids are safer in pregnancy
No change is needed before conception, as methotrexate is cleared rapidly and poses no fetal risk
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Methotrexate is an abortifacient causing multiple malformations and must be stopped before conception — at least 3 months, or 1 month in women per UK guidance
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Methotrexate is an abortifacient causing multiple malformations and must be stopped before conception. The conventional advice is at least 3 months; current UK rheumatology guidance supports 1 month in women and 3 months in men.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which drug, associated with severe CNS/cardiac/craniofacial defects, requires patients to be enrolled in a strict pregnancy-prevention programme?
options: Paracetamol
Cefalexin
Isotretinoin (a retinoid)
Labetalol
Nifedipine
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Isotretinoin (a retinoid)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Isotretinoin (a retinoid) causes severe CNS/cardiac/craniofacial defects and requires a strict pregnancy-prevention programme.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A pregnant woman needs an antibiotic. Which agent is associated with tooth discolouration and impaired fetal bone growth, and what should be used instead?
options: Penicillin; use a tetracycline instead
Cefalexin; use gentamicin instead
Amoxicillin; use trimethoprim instead
Nitrofurantoin; use a tetracycline instead
A tetracycline (e.g. doxycycline); use penicillins/cephalosporins instead
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: A tetracycline (e.g. doxycycline); use penicillins/cephalosporins instead
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Tetracyclines (e.g. doxycycline) cause tooth discolouration and impaired bone growth if given from the 2nd trimester, but they are avoided throughout pregnancy. Penicillins/cephalosporins are the safe alternatives.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which class of antibiotic is associated with fetal ototoxicity (CN VIII damage → deafness)?
options: Penicillins
Aminoglycosides (e.g. gentamicin)
Cephalosporins
Macrolides
Nitrofurantoin
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Aminoglycosides (e.g. gentamicin)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Aminoglycosides (e.g. gentamicin) cause ototoxicity — CN VIII damage leading to deafness.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A woman in her first trimester has a UTI. Why is trimethoprim avoided, and which agent is preferred?
options: It causes neonatal haemolysis in the first trimester; use nitrofurantoin throughout pregnancy including at term
It causes ototoxicity and eighth nerve damage; use gentamicin instead, with serum level monitoring
It causes tooth discolouration and impaired bone growth; use doxycycline, which is safe in pregnancy
It is a folate antagonist causing neural tube defects; use nitrofurantoin (first choice, but not at term), or cefalexin/amoxicillin
It is entirely safe in pregnancy and should be used first line, with no need for an alternative agent
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: It is a folate antagonist causing neural tube defects; use nitrofurantoin (first choice, but not at term), or cefalexin/amoxicillin
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist causing NTDs in the 1st trimester. Nitrofurantoin is the first-choice antibiotic for lower UTI in pregnancy, avoided at term (neonatal haemolysis) and in G6PD deficiency, with cefalexin or amoxicillin (if susceptible) as second choice (NICE).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Nitrofurantoin is generally safe earlier in pregnancy but should be avoided at term. Why?
options: It can cause neonatal haemolysis if used at term (3rd trimester)
It causes neural tube defects at term
It causes premature ductus arteriosus closure
It causes ototoxicity
It causes tooth discolouration
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: It can cause neonatal haemolysis if used at term (3rd trimester)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Nitrofurantoin can cause neonatal haemolysis if used at term (3rd trimester), so it is avoided then although safe earlier in pregnancy.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A pregnant woman near term takes an NSAID for pain. What is the characteristic fetal risk, and what is the safe analgesic alternative?
options: Neural tube defects (and spina bifida); use high-dose folic acid
Sensorineural deafness (and vestibular damage); use gentamicin
Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus (and oligohydramnios); use paracetamol
Ebstein's anomaly of the tricuspid valve; use lithium instead
Tooth discolouration (and impaired bone growth); use a tetracycline
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus (and oligohydramnios); use paracetamol
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: NSAIDs are avoided from 20 weeks (MHRA) because of oligohydramnios and fetal renal impairment, and especially in the 3rd trimester, when they cause premature closure of the ductus arteriosus. Paracetamol is the safe alternative. Low-dose aspirin is the exception, used deliberately from 12 weeks for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis in women at increased risk (NICE).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A woman with hyperthyroidism becomes pregnant while on carbimazole. What fetal harm is associated with carbimazole, and what is preferred in the first trimester?
options: Ototoxicity and eighth nerve damage; switch to gentamicin for the first trimester
Ebstein's anomaly of the tricuspid valve; continue carbimazole throughout pregnancy
Neural tube defects and spina bifida; add high-dose folic acid and continue carbimazole
Phocomelia and limb reduction defects; switch to thalidomide for the first trimester
Aplasia cutis and choanal/oesophageal atresia; switch to propylthiouracil in the first trimester
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Aplasia cutis and choanal/oesophageal atresia; switch to propylthiouracil in the first trimester
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Carbimazole is associated with aplasia cutis and choanal/oesophageal atresia, so propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester. Consider switching back to carbimazole afterwards, as propylthiouracil risks liver injury. Neither drug is risk-free — use the lowest effective dose under specialist care.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which historical drug is the archetype of teratogenicity, and what limb malformation does it cause?
options: Warfarin; nasal hypoplasia
Thalidomide; phocomelia (limb defects)
Valproate; spina bifida
Lithium; Ebstein's anomaly
Isotretinoin; craniofacial defects
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Thalidomide; phocomelia (limb defects)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Thalidomide is the historical archetype of teratogenicity, causing phocomelia (limb defects).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which set of drugs is associated with harm specifically in the 2nd/3rd trimester (growth/functional/organ damage)?
options: Valproate, warfarin, methotrexate and retinoids, all causing functional organ damage late in pregnancy
Lithium, trimethoprim and isotretinoin, all causing growth restriction in the second and third trimesters
Lamotrigine, levetiracetam and folic acid, all causing functional organ damage in later pregnancy
ACEi/ARB (renal), tetracyclines (teeth/bone), NSAIDs (ductus arteriosus), nitrofurantoin at term (haemolysis)
Paracetamol, penicillin and cefalexin, all causing growth restriction in the second and third trimesters
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: ACEi/ARB (renal), tetracyclines (teeth/bone), NSAIDs (ductus arteriosus), nitrofurantoin at term (haemolysis)
