conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: 2nd/3rd trimester harm (growth/functional/organ damage) is characteristic of ACEi/ARB (renal), tetracyclines (teeth/bone), NSAIDs (ductus arteriosus), and nitrofurantoin at term (haemolysis). Valproate, warfarin, methotrexate and retinoids cause 1st-trimester structural malformations. Note that tetracyclines are in fact avoided throughout pregnancy — the dental effect is simply the 2nd/3rd-trimester one — and NSAIDs are avoided from 20 weeks, not just the 3rd trimester.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which general principle should guide prescribing in pregnancy?
options: Prescribe only if benefit outweighs risk, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and prefer drugs with a long safety record
Always use the highest tolerated dose to guarantee efficacy, since undertreatment is the greater risk
Never check pregnancy status before prescribing, as this delays treatment in women of childbearing age
Prefer newer drugs, which are always safer in pregnancy than long-established alternatives
Avoid consulting the BNF or a specialist service, since pregnancy advice changes too often to be useful
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Prescribe only if benefit outweighs risk, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and prefer drugs with a long safety record
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Prescribe in pregnancy only if benefit outweighs risk, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and prefer drugs with a long safety record. Always check pregnancy status, counsel pre-conception, and consult the BNF/UKTIS when unsure.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the overriding principle in the initial management of a poisoned patient?
options: Give a specific antidote immediately in every case
Always perform haemodialysis
Give activated charcoal regardless of the poison
Resuscitation first (A–E), supporting physiology, as most poisonings are managed supportively
Induce vomiting
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Resuscitation first (A–E), supporting physiology, as most poisonings are managed supportively
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The poisoned patient is managed with resuscitation first (A–E), supporting physiology rather than relying on antidotes — most poisonings are managed supportively.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Activated charcoal is being considered for a poisoned patient. Which of the following is it useless against?
options: Metals, alcohols, and lithium
Aspirin taken 30 minutes ago
Tricyclic antidepressants taken within an hour
Paracetamol within an hour
Most oral drugs with a protected airway
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Metals, alcohols, and lithium
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Activated charcoal 50 g (adult) is given within 1 hour of ingestion (later for modified-release preparations), only if the airway is protected, and is avoided in corrosives, hydrocarbons and bowel obstruction. It doesn't bind everything — it is useless for metals, alcohols and lithium.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following poisons is dialysable by haemodialysis?
options: Tricyclic antidepressants
Benzodiazepines
Salicylates, lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol, and theophylline
Iron
Digoxin
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Salicylates, lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol, and theophylline
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The dialysable poisons are salicylates, lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol, and theophylline.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A farm worker presents with pinpoint pupils, salivation, lacrimation, urination, defaecation, bradycardia and bronchorrhoea. Which toxidrome and cause is this?
options: Anticholinergic; TCA overdose
Opioid; heroin
Sympathomimetic; cocaine
Serotonergic; SSRI
Cholinergic; organophosphate poisoning
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Cholinergic; organophosphate poisoning
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: This is the cholinergic toxidrome — small pupils (miosis), SLUD, bradycardia and bronchorrhoea ('wet') — caused by organophosphates. The highest-yield discriminator is 'wet + small pupils' = cholinergic.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient is dry, hot, flushed and delirious with large pupils, urinary retention and tachycardia. Which toxidrome is this, and what is a typical cause?
options: Cholinergic; organophosphates
Anticholinergic; TCAs, antihistamines, or atropine
Opioid; morphine
Serotonergic; tramadol
Sympathomimetic; amphetamines
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Anticholinergic; TCAs, antihistamines, or atropine
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The anticholinergic toxidrome features large pupils (mydriasis), a dry, hot, flushed patient with delirium, retention and tachycardia — caused by TCAs, antihistamines or atropine. 'Dry + large pupils' = anticholinergic.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the single highest-yield discriminator between the cholinergic and anticholinergic toxidromes?
options: Heart rate alone, since one toxidrome causes bradycardia and the other tachycardia
The presence of seizures, which occur in one toxidrome and never in the other
Blood pressure
'Wet vs dry': cholinergic = wet + small pupils; anticholinergic = dry + large pupils
Body temperature only
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: 'Wet vs dry': cholinergic = wet + small pupils; anticholinergic = dry + large pupils
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The 'wet vs dry' rule is the single highest-yield discriminator: cholinergic = wet (salivation, lacrimation, sweating, diarrhoea) with small pupils (organophosphates); anticholinergic = dry with large pupils (TCA/antihistamine).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How does paracetamol cause hepatotoxicity, and which patient group is at higher risk?
options: Via the toxic metabolite NAPQI; higher risk with chronic alcohol, anorexia (reduced glutathione) and P450 inducers (increased NAPQI)
Direct hepatocyte necrosis from the parent drug; risk is highest in young, otherwise healthy patients
By causing cholestasis; risk in obesity
Through an immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction; risk is highest in atopic patients
By raising ammonia; risk in renal failure
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Via the toxic metabolite NAPQI; higher risk with chronic alcohol, anorexia (reduced glutathione) and P450 inducers (increased NAPQI)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Paracetamol causes hepatotoxicity via NAPQI (a toxic metabolite). Malnutrition and anorexia deplete glutathione; P450 inducers increase NAPQI production. Since the move to a single treatment line, these risk factors guide clinical concern but no longer change the treatment line (MHRA).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient presents 6 hours after a single (non-staggered) paracetamol overdose. How should treatment be guided?
options: Give N-acetylcysteine only if the patient becomes symptomatic or jaundiced over the next 24 hours
Measure the level immediately at presentation and treat if any level is detectable
Measure the level now (already ≥4 hours post-ingestion) and plot on the nomogram; treat if on or above the line
Give activated charcoal regardless of timing, since it binds paracetamol at any point after ingestion
Discharge if asymptomatic
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Measure the level now (already ≥4 hours post-ingestion) and plot on the nomogram; treat if on or above the line
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: For a non-staggered overdose the level is valid from 4 hours onwards — measured earlier it is unreliable — so at 6 hours it is taken immediately and plotted on the nomogram. Acetylcysteine is given if the level is on or above the single treatment line. Liver damage peaks at 72–96h, and early acetylcysteine saves lives.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which set of criteria indicates the need for liver transplant referral in paracetamol overdose (King's College criteria)?
options: Any detectable paracetamol level on the admission blood sample, whatever the timing
Nausea and vomiting alone
A single raised ALT at presentation, before any acetylcysteine has been given
RUQ pain at 24 hours
Arterial pH <7.3 beyond 24h, OR all three of PT >100s + creatinine >300 micromol/L + grade 3/4 encephalopathy
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Arterial pH <7.3 beyond 24h, OR all three of PT >100s + creatinine >300 micromol/L + grade 3/4 encephalopathy
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Early discussion with a liver unit is indicated if arterial pH is <7.3 more than 24h after ingestion (after fluid resuscitation), OR all three of PT >100s, creatinine >300 micromol/L, and grade 3/4 encephalopathy. These are referral criteria, not a decision to transplant.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient with a salicylate (aspirin) overdose has tinnitus and is hyperventilating. What is the characteristic sequence of acid-base disturbance?
options: Metabolic acidosis first, then respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis first (hyperventilation stimulates the medulla), then metabolic acidosis (lactic acid)
Respiratory acidosis only, from direct depression of the respiratory centre
Metabolic alkalosis only, from vomiting and loss of gastric acid
No acid-base disturbance
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Respiratory alkalosis first (hyperventilation stimulates the medulla), then metabolic acidosis (lactic acid)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Salicylate overdose causes a mixed disorder: respiratory alkalosis first (aspirin stimulates the medullary respiratory centre), then metabolic acidosis (lactic acid accumulation).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How does urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate help in salicylate overdose?
options: It binds salicylate in the gut
It reverses the respiratory alkalosis
It replenishes glutathione
It traps ionised salicylate in the urine, increasing its excretion
It chelates the salicylate
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: It traps ionised salicylate in the urine, increasing its excretion
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: IV sodium bicarbonate causes urinary alkalinisation, which traps ionised salicylate in the urine and increases its excretion. Hypokalaemia must be corrected first, or alkalinisation fails. Haemodialysis is indicated if concentration >700mg/L, metabolic acidosis, ARF, pulmonary oedema, or seizures.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient presents with pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and drowsiness. What is the emergency antidote, and what caution applies?
options: Naloxone 400 micrograms IV, repeated every 2–3 minutes up to 10 mg, titrated to respiratory rate; short-acting, so re-narcotisation may occur
Flumazenil, titrated to conscious level; the caution is precipitating seizures in dependence
N-acetylcysteine, given over one hour; the caution is an anaphylactoid infusion reaction
Atropine; titrate to dry secretions
Intralipid; the lipid sink
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Naloxone 400 micrograms IV, repeated every 2–3 minutes up to 10 mg, titrated to respiratory rate; short-acting, so re-narcotisation may occur
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The opioid triad (pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, drowsiness) is reversed with naloxone — 400 micrograms IV initially, repeated at 2–3 minute intervals up to a maximum of 10 mg (BNF), titrated to respiratory rate rather than consciousness. Use about 100 microgram increments in opioid-dependent or palliative patients. It is short-acting, so repeat doses or an infusion may be needed for a long-acting opioid — monitor for re-narcotisation.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient with a tricyclic antidepressant overdose has a widened QRS on ECG. What is the first-line treatment and its mechanism?
options: Flumazenil; reverses the TCA
Naloxone; competes at receptors
IV sodium bicarbonate; alkalinises plasma, reducing free TCA and narrowing the QRS
Atropine; treats the tachycardia
Activated charcoal alone regardless of timing
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: IV sodium bicarbonate; alkalinises plasma, reducing free TCA and narrowing the QRS
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: TCA overdose is cardiotoxic — a wide QRS is the key marker. IV sodium bicarbonate is first-line: it alkalinises the plasma to pH 7.45–7.55, reducing free TCA and narrowing the QRS. It is the treatment rather than an antiarrhythmic, and antiarrhythmic drugs must NOT be given as they worsen sodium-channel blockade. Flumazenil should not be given either (a benzodiazepine might coexist; seizure risk).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which antidote reverses benzodiazepine overdose, and what is the key caution?
options: Naloxone, given by IV or IM injection; the caution is re-narcotisation as it wears off
Atropine; caution tachycardia
Sodium bicarbonate; caution alkalosis
Desferrioxamine by IV infusion; the caution is hypotension if infused too rapidly
Flumazenil (antagonist at the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A) — but rarely used, because of seizure risk
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Flumazenil (antagonist at the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A) — but rarely used, because of seizure risk
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Benzodiazepine overdose is managed supportively; flumazenil is an antagonist at the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor but is rarely given in UK practice, because it precipitates seizures in mixed or unknown overdose, TCA co-ingestion, epilepsy and benzodiazepine dependence.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient rescued from a house fire has headache and confusion, with a normal-reading pulse oximeter. Why is the SpO₂ misleading, and what is the treatment?
options: The SpO₂ is accurate and reassuring, so the patient can be managed on room air with observation
Oximetry can't distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin, so SpO₂ is falsely normal; give high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask
SpO₂ overreads; give diuretics
SpO₂ is low; give naloxone
The SpO₂ is irrelevant in inhalational poisoning; give activated charcoal to bind the toxin
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Oximetry can't distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin, so SpO₂ is falsely normal; give high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: In CO poisoning, SpO₂ is falsely normal because oximetry can't distinguish CO-Hb (co-oximetry is needed) — this is the discriminator. Treatment is high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreathe reservoir mask (shortens CO-Hb t½ from ~5h to ~90min), with hyperbaric O₂ if severe or in pregnancy. Cherry-red skin is a late/post-mortem sign and its absence excludes nothing.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: In organophosphate poisoning, what are the first-line and additional antidotes?
options: Naloxone first-line to reverse the cholinergic excess; flumazenil if the patient presents early
Sodium bicarbonate first-line; charcoal if late
Desferrioxamine first-line; dialysis if severe
Atropine first-line (titrated until secretions dry) and pralidoxime (regenerates AChE) if given early
Intralipid first-line, using the lipid sink to sequester the lipophilic organophosphate
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Atropine first-line (titrated until secretions dry) and pralidoxime (regenerates AChE) if given early
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing ACh excess (SLUD, bradycardia, miosis, bronchospasm). Atropine is first-line — 1.2–2 mg IV, doubled every 3–5 minutes until secretions dry, and pralidoxime (which regenerates AChE) is given early.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient who drank antifreeze develops CNS depression then a raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and renal failure. What is the poison, and how is it treated?
options: Ethylene glycol; treat with fomepizole (or ethanol) plus haemodialysis
Methanol; treat with naloxone
Iron; treat with desferrioxamine
Lithium; treat with fluids
Cyanide; treat with hydroxocobalamin
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Ethylene glycol; treat with fomepizole (or ethanol) plus haemodialysis
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Ethylene glycol (antifreeze) causes initial CNS depression, then a raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and renal failure (converted to oxalic acid). Treatment is fomepizole (alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor, first-line) or ethanol infusion, plus haemodialysis.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient presents with a raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and visual loss/blindness after ingesting a toxic alcohol. Which poison is this, and what is the mechanism of the eye toxicity?
options: Ethylene glycol; oxalate crystals in the eye
Iron; retinal deposition
Methanol; optic nerve toxicity from formic acid
Lithium; papilloedema
Cyanide; retinal ischaemia
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Methanol; optic nerve toxicity from formic acid
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Methanol poisoning presents like ethylene glycol but with the hallmark of visual loss/blindness due to optic nerve toxicity from formic acid. The pairing is: glycol → renal failure, methanol → blindness. Treatment is fomepizole/ethanol + haemodialysis.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A toddler with accidental iron overdose has vomiting and haematemesis, then a latent phase, then shock and hepatotoxicity. What is the antidote, and does charcoal help?
options: Naloxone; charcoal binds iron well
Fomepizole; charcoal is first-line
Atropine; charcoal is essential
Intralipid; charcoal is helpful
Desferrioxamine (a chelator); charcoal does not bind iron
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Desferrioxamine (a chelator); charcoal does not bind iron
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Iron overdose progresses through GI symptoms → latent phase → shock + hepatotoxicity (with later bowel strictures). The antidote is desferrioxamine (a chelator); activated charcoal does not bind iron.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on lithium becomes dehydrated after starting a thiazide and develops a coarse tremor, ataxia and confusion. Which factors precipitate lithium toxicity, and how is it managed?
options: Precipitated by strenuous exercise and managed with flumazenil to reverse the sedation
Precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi and thiazides; managed with IV 0.9% saline and haemodialysis if severe — no antidote
Precipitated by a high protein intake and managed with repeated doses of activated charcoal
Precipitated by alkalosis; managed with naloxone
Precipitated by nothing; it has a wide therapeutic index
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi and thiazides; managed with IV 0.9% saline and haemodialysis if severe — no antidote
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index; toxicity (coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, seizures, renal impairment) is precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi and thiazides. There is no specific antidote — manage with IV 0.9% saline and haemodialysis if severe.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: During a regional anaesthetic, a patient develops perioral tingling, tinnitus, seizures and cardiac arrest after inadvertent IV bupivacaine. What is the antidote?
options: Naloxone
Atropine
Sodium bicarbonate
IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid) — the 'lipid sink'
Flumazenil
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid) — the 'lipid sink'
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Local anaesthetic toxicity (perioral tingling, tinnitus, seizures, cardiac arrest, e.g. from inadvertent IV bupivacaine) is treated with IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid) — the 'lipid sink'.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient rescued from a house fire has a high lactate, cardiovascular collapse, reduced GCS and a bitter-almond smell despite already receiving high-flow oxygen. Which additional poison is this, and its antidote?
options: Cyanide; hydroxocobalamin
Carbon monoxide; 100% oxygen
Methanol; fomepizole
Iron; desferrioxamine
Lithium; haemodialysis
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Cyanide; hydroxocobalamin
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Cyanide poisoning (smoke inhalation/industrial) presents with headache, reduced GCS, high lactate, cardiovascular collapse and a classic bitter-almond smell. The antidote is hydroxocobalamin; dicobalt edetate is reserved for confirmed poisoning, being itself toxic if cyanide is absent. Carbon monoxide usually coexists and high-flow oxygen is given for both.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on an SSRI is given tramadol and develops tremor, clonus, hyperreflexia, dilated pupils and hyperthermia. What is the diagnosis, and its management?
options: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; dantrolene only
Anticholinergic toxidrome; physostigmine
Serotonin syndrome; stop the serotonergic drugs, then supportive care, with cyproheptadine if severe
Malignant hyperthermia triggered by the tramadol; treat with dantrolene and active cooling
Opioid toxicity from the tramadol; treat with naloxone titrated to respiratory rate
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Serotonin syndrome; stop the serotonergic drugs, then supportive care, with cyproheptadine if severe
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Serotonin syndrome results from excess serotonergic activity (e.g. SSRI + tramadol) — clonus, hyperreflexia, dilated pupils, hyperthermia. Management begins with stopping the serotonergic drugs, then supportive care (IV fluids, cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation), with cyproheptadine (a 5-HT2 antagonist) on specialist advice if severe.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How can serotonin syndrome, neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) and the anticholinergic toxidrome be distinguished by neurological signs?
options: All three cause identical signs, so the distinction rests entirely on the drug history
Serotonin syndrome causes rigidity; NMS causes clonus
Anticholinergic causes hyperreflexia; NMS causes flushing
They cannot be distinguished clinically and require muscle biopsy to tell them apart
Serotonin = clonus/hyperreflexia/mydriasis; NMS = lead-pipe rigidity/bradyreflexia; anticholinergic = dry/flushed/normal reflexes
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Serotonin = clonus/hyperreflexia/mydriasis; NMS = lead-pipe rigidity/bradyreflexia; anticholinergic = dry/flushed/normal reflexes
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Serotonin syndrome shows clonus/hyperreflexia/mydriasis; NMS shows lead-pipe rigidity/bradyreflexia (from antipsychotics); the anticholinergic toxidrome is dry/flushed with normal reflexes.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient with a beta-blocker overdose has refractory bradycardia not responding to atropine. Which antidote is used, and by what mechanism?
options: Naloxone; reverses at opioid receptors
High-dose glucagon; increases cAMP independent of beta-receptors
Flumazenil; reverses at GABA receptors
Desferrioxamine; chelates the drug
Intralipid; the lipid sink
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: High-dose glucagon; increases cAMP independent of beta-receptors
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: In beta-blocker overdose, atropine is used for bradycardia, and glucagon 5–10 mg IV over 1–2 minutes (then an infusion) increases cAMP independent of beta-receptors. (Calcium gluconate is used for calcium-channel blocker overdose.)

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following best defines an adverse drug reaction (ADR)?
options: Any harm associated with a drug, including harm arising from a prescribing or administration error
A response occurring only after an overdose, when the dose exceeds the normal therapeutic range
A harmless expected effect of a drug that causes no clinical problem and needs no action
A noxious and unintended response to a drug at normal therapeutic doses, distinct from overdose/toxicity and medication errors
Any error made during the prescribing process, whether or not it reaches or harms the patient
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: A noxious and unintended response to a drug at normal therapeutic doses, distinct from overdose/toxicity and medication errors
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: An ADR is a noxious + unintended response to a drug at normal therapeutic doses — distinct from overdose/toxicity and from medication errors. (An adverse drug event is the broader term that includes harm from medication error.)

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: How does an 'adverse drug event' differ from an ADR?
options: An adverse drug event is any harm associated with a drug, including from medication error, and is therefore broader than an ADR
They are identical terms for the same thing, used interchangeably in pharmacovigilance
An adverse drug event only occurs at high doses, whereas an ADR occurs at normal therapeutic doses
An adverse drug event excludes medication errors, making it narrower than an adverse drug reaction
An ADR is broader than an adverse drug event, because it includes harm from errors and overdose
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: An adverse drug event is any harm associated with a drug, including from medication error, and is therefore broader than an ADR
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: An adverse drug event is any harm associated with a drug, including from medication error, making it broader than an ADR (which occurs at normal doses). A side effect is a known, often predictable secondary effect — a subset of ADRs.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following meets the MHRA definition of a serious ADR?
options: Mild transient nausea
A predictable dose-related headache
An ADR that causes or prolongs hospitalisation
A minor rash that resolves quickly
Any side effect listed in the BNF
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: An ADR that causes or prolongs hospitalisation
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The MHRA defines a serious ADR as one that is fatal, life-threatening, disabling/incapacitating, causes/prolongs hospitalisation, causes a congenital abnormality, or is otherwise medically significant.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on a β-blocker develops bradycardia, and another on insulin develops hypoglycaemia. Which Rawlins-Thompson type do these represent?
options: Type B (Bizarre) — unpredictable and immune-mediated
Type C (Chronic)
Type D (Delayed)
Type E (End-of-use)
Type A (Augmented) — dose-dependent, predictable exaggeration of the drug's action
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Type A (Augmented) — dose-dependent, predictable exaggeration of the drug's action
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type A (Augmented) ADRs are dose-dependent, predictable exaggerations of the drug's action — e.g. β-blocker → bradycardia, opioid → respiratory depression, insulin → hypoglycaemia, anticoagulant → bleeding. Type A is the commonest; case-fatality per reaction is low, but because Type A reactions are so common they cause most ADR admissions and deaths.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient develops anaphylaxis after penicillin, and another develops Stevens-Johnson syndrome on carbamazepine. Which Rawlins-Thompson type is this, and what are its features?
options: Type A — dose-dependent and predictable
Type B (Bizarre) — not dose-dependent, unpredictable, often immune-mediated, high mortality
Type C (Chronic) — dose and time-dependent
Type D (Delayed)
Type E (End-of-use)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Type B (Bizarre) — not dose-dependent, unpredictable, often immune-mediated, high mortality
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type B (Bizarre) ADRs are not dose-dependent, unpredictable, often immune-mediated, and carry high mortality — e.g. penicillin anaphylaxis, malignant hyperthermia, carbamazepine → SJS, and Reye's syndrome with aspirin.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient on long-term steroids develops osteoporosis with a vertebral fragility fracture. Which type of ADR is this?
options: Type A (Augmented)
Type B (Bizarre)
Type D (Delayed)
Type C (Chronic/Continued) — dose and time-dependent with prolonged use
Type E (End-of-use)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Type C (Chronic/Continued) — dose and time-dependent with prolonged use
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type C (Chronic/Continued) ADRs are dose- and time-dependent, occurring with prolonged use — e.g. steroids → osteoporosis, and bisphosphonates → osteonecrosis of the jaw. Iatrogenic Cushing's, by contrast, is Type A: an exaggeration of the drug's own glucocorticoid action.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Thalidomide causing teratogenesis, and tardive dyskinesia appearing after long-term antipsychotic use, are examples of which ADR type?
options: Type D (Delayed) — appears long after exposure
Type A (Augmented)
Type C (Chronic)
Type E (End-of-use)
Type B (Bizarre)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Type D (Delayed) — appears long after exposure
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type D (Delayed) ADRs appear long after exposure — e.g. teratogenesis (thalidomide), carcinogenesis (secondary malignancy after chemotherapy/radiotherapy) and tardive dyskinesia. (Carbimazole → agranulocytosis is instead a Type B (Bizarre), idiosyncratic reaction.)

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: A patient who abruptly stops long-term steroids develops an adrenal crisis. Which Rawlins-Thompson type is this?
options: Type A (Augmented)
Type C (Chronic)
Type E (End-of-use/withdrawal) — on stopping, especially abruptly
Type D (Delayed)
Type B (Bizarre)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Type E (End-of-use/withdrawal) — on stopping, especially abruptly
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type E (End-of-use/withdrawal) ADRs occur on stopping a drug, especially abruptly — e.g. steroid withdrawal → adrenal crisis, benzodiazepine/opioid withdrawal, and β-blocker rebound.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the key conceptual split between Type A and Type B ADRs, and how does management differ?
options: Type A is immune and Type B is dose-dependent; both need the drug stopped and permanently avoided thereafter
Both are unpredictable and require the drug to be avoided permanently, with the reaction documented as an allergy
Type A occurs only on withdrawal and Type B only on starting; both are managed by adjusting the dose
There is no meaningful difference in management — both are handled by reducing the dose and monitoring
Type A is predictable and dose-dependent; Type B is unpredictable and immune, needing permanent avoidance
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Type A is predictable and dose-dependent; Type B is unpredictable and immune, needing permanent avoidance
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Type A = predictable + dose-dependent (the bulk of ADRs — reduce the dose if mild, but stop the drug and treat actively if severe, as in opioid respiratory depression or major bleeding). Type B = unpredictable + immune — stop the drug, avoid it and cross-reacting drugs permanently, and document it as an allergy.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following is a recognised risk factor for ADRs?
options: Young healthy adults on a single drug with normal renal and hepatic function
Polypharmacy, extremes of age, organ impairment, female sex, and genetic factors (e.g. CYP polymorphisms, G6PD)
Taking exactly one medication, with no comorbidity and no relevant genetic variation
Normal renal and hepatic function, with no polypharmacy and no extremes of age
Absence of comorbidities, normal organ function and no concurrent prescribed medicines
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Polypharmacy, extremes of age, organ impairment, female sex, and genetic factors (e.g. CYP polymorphisms, G6PD)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Risk factors for ADRs include extremes of age (altered PK), polypharmacy (interaction risk), organ impairment (renal/hepatic), female sex, genetic factors (CYP polymorphisms, G6PD), and multiple comorbidities.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: When assessing whether a drug caused a reaction, symptoms improve when the drug is stopped and recur when it is restarted. What are these two steps called?
options: Titration and tapering
Induction and inhibition
Loading and maintenance
Dechallenge (improvement on stopping) and rechallenge (recurrence on restarting)
Sensitisation and desensitisation
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Dechallenge (improvement on stopping) and rechallenge (recurrence on restarting)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Causality assessment uses the temporal relationship, the known reaction profile, improvement on stopping (dechallenge) and recurrence on restarting (rechallenge), and exclusion of other causes — formalised by scales such as Naranjo. Rechallenge is usually only observed inadvertently: deliberate rechallenge is contraindicated after any serious or Type B reaction — anaphylaxis, SJS/TEN, DRESS and agranulocytosis are never re-exposed.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which drug–ADR pairing is a recognised 'classic culprit'?
options: ACE inhibitors → cough/angioedema
Statins → hypoglycaemia
Amiodarone → single-organ effect only
Methotrexate → gingival hyperplasia
Insulin → myopathy
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: ACE inhibitors → cough/angioedema
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Classic culprit ADRs include ACE inhibitors → dry cough and angioedema, statins → myopathy, amiodarone → multi-organ effects, and methotrexate → marrow/liver toxicity. The cough is benign and prompts a switch to an ARB; angioedema is an airway emergency that permanently contraindicates ACE inhibitors. Gingival hyperplasia belongs to phenytoin, ciclosporin and nifedipine, not methotrexate.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: What is the primary purpose of the Yellow Card scheme, and who runs it?
options: Pre-marketing clinical trial approval and licensing of new medicines, run by NICE
Prescription cost monitoring and formulary control across the NHS, run by NHS England
Post-marketing pharmacovigilance (drug-safety surveillance after licensing), run by the MHRA (+ Commission on Human Medicines)
Drug manufacturing quality control and batch release testing, run by the manufacturer
Patient complaint handling about prescribing decisions, run by the local health board
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Post-marketing pharmacovigilance (drug-safety surveillance after licensing), run by the MHRA (+ Commission on Human Medicines)
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The Yellow Card scheme is the UK system for post-marketing pharmacovigilance (drug-safety surveillance after licensing), run by the MHRA and the Commission on Human Medicines. It detects rare or delayed ADRs that trials are too small/short to find.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Who is permitted to submit a Yellow Card report, and is proof of causation required?
options: Only doctors may report, and causation must be proven before a report is submitted
Only the MHRA itself, drawing on data submitted by marketing authorisation holders
Only the drug manufacturer, who must then forward confirmed reports to the regulator
Only hospital pharmacists, with documented proof of causation required for each report
Anyone — doctors, pharmacists, nurses, and patients/carers — voluntarily, on suspicion, with no proof of causation needed
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Anyone — doctors, pharmacists, nurses, and patients/carers — voluntarily, on suspicion, with no proof of causation needed
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Anyone can report — doctors, pharmacists, nurses, and patients/carers — voluntarily. No proof of causation is needed; reports are made on suspicion.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: For a newly-licensed drug marked with a black triangle (▼), which reactions should be reported via Yellow Card?
options: Only serious reactions
All reactions, however minor, because the drug is under additional monitoring
Only reactions in children
Only reactions already well-recognised
No reactions unless fatal
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: All reactions, however minor, because the drug is under additional monitoring
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: The black triangle (▼) marks newly-licensed drugs/vaccines (and biosimilars) under intensive/additional monitoring — all reactions should be reported, however minor.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: For an established (non-black-triangle) drug, which suspected ADRs should always be reported?
options: Only mild, well-recognised reactions, since serious ones will already be known to the manufacturer
No reactions at all — established medicines are outside the scheme once they are no longer new
Only reactions the manufacturer specifically requests, as they hold the marketing authorisation
All serious suspected ADRs, all suspected ADRs in children under 18, and suspected ADRs in pregnancy
Only reactions occurring within 24 hours of the dose, since later events cannot be attributed to the drug
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: All serious suspected ADRs, all suspected ADRs in children under 18, and suspected ADRs in pregnancy
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Always report: all serious suspected ADRs to established drugs (even if well-recognised), all suspected ADRs in children (<18, even off-label), suspected ADRs in pregnancy (however minor), and delayed reactions such as cancers/fibrosis (even years later).

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which of the following is reportable via the Yellow Card scheme?
options: Reactions to any therapeutic agent, plus medical devices, defective and falsified products, and e-cigarettes
Only prescribed medicines — OTC purchases, vaccines, herbal products and devices are outside the scheme
Only injectable drugs, since oral formulations rarely cause reactions serious enough to report
Only drugs bought in a pharmacy, since prescribed medicines are already monitored by the prescriber
Only drugs given in hospital, since community reactions are handled by the manufacturer instead
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Reactions to any therapeutic agent, plus medical devices, defective and falsified products, and e-cigarettes
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: Yellow Card reporting covers reactions to any therapeutic agent — prescribed and OTC/self-medication, vaccines, blood products, radiographic contrast, herbal/complementary and homeopathic products — and also medical devices (including software and apps), defective medicines, falsified (fake) medicines and devices, and e-cigarettes and e-liquids. It is not limited to prescribed drugs.

conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.question: Which set of measures helps minimise ADRs in prescribing?
options: Maximise the number of drugs to cover every symptom, and avoid taking a drug history as it delays treatment
Prescribe high doses from the outset in the elderly, since reduced absorption makes standard doses ineffective
Take a full drug and allergy history, deprescribe, check interactions, start low and go slow, and reconcile at transitions
Never document allergies, to save time at admission and avoid withholding drugs unnecessarily
Avoid monitoring high-risk drugs, since levels rarely change once a patient is established on treatment
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.answer: Take a full drug and allergy history, deprescribe, check interactions, start low and go slow, and reconcile at transitions
conditions__CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRES.explanation: ADRs are minimised by taking a full drug + allergy history (incl. OTC/herbal), avoiding polypharmacy (deprescribing), checking interactions (BNF), starting low and going slow in the elderly/organ impairment, using the fewest drugs, monitoring high-risk drugs, documenting/communicating allergies, and medication reconciliation at transitions of care.
